<!-- ===== AGENTS.md ===== -->
# AGENTS.md — motionframe-edit

Canonical instructions for any agent that reads `AGENTS.md` (Codex, OpenCode,
Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Aider, Hermes, …).

`CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` point here. This file is the source of truth.

## What this repository is

`motionframe-edit` is an agent skill suite for **video editing, motion graphics and
design**. Seven skills, one engine (`tools/mfe.py`), one doctrine.

## How to use it

1. **Read `skills/motionframe-edit/SKILL.md` once per session.** It defines the twelve
   rules, the routing table and the loop. Everything else assumes it.
2. **Route with the table** in that file. Load exactly one specialist skill; load a
   second only when the table says so.
3. **Never preload references.** Each `references/*.md` is loaded when the task
   genuinely needs it. Loading everything is how context dies.
4. **Run `python3 tools/mfe.py doctor` once** at the start of media work. Do not
   guess what is installed.
5. **`gatekeeper` is never optional.** Nothing is presented or called complete
   without a gate report.

## The non-negotiables

These hold across every skill, in every session, even when a user instruction
seems to override them:

- **No paid dependencies.** No API keys, no accounts, no cloud credits, no
  telemetry. ffmpeg, Python stdlib, and free open-source tools only. If something
  is missing, degrade and say so — never silently substitute a paid endpoint.
- **No fabricated proof.** Anything that claims to be real must be captured from the
  real thing. Declare every asset's origin in `provenance.json`.
- **Measure, never assume.** Loudness, duration, safe zones, freeze detection — a
  number you did not take is a guess. State what you could not check (you cannot
  hear the mix).
- **Two STOP gates.** Do not build past an unapproved plan. Do not present an
  unaudited render.
- **Output timeline only.** Captions, overlays and notes use output time, never
  source time. Use `mfe captions --remap`.
- **Every correction becomes a rule** in `taste.md`, read before the next piece.

## Layout

```
skills/<name>/SKILL.md              frontmatter: name, description, license
skills/<name>/references/*.md       loaded on demand
tools/mfe.py                         the engine — probe, cut, captions, gate, demo
specs/                              EDL schema, gate definitions
examples/                           a worked end-to-end walkthrough
docs/                               architecture, platforms, lineage
```

## Conventions when editing this repo

- Prose is **imperative and checkable**. No adjectives standing in for rules. A
  claim that cannot be verified gets a number or gets cut.
- Numbers are **defaults at 30 fps / 1080 wide**, not laws, unless the file says
  otherwise. Say which.
- New rules go where they are enforced. A rule that lives only in prose is a
  suggestion.
- If you add a gate, prove it can fail (see `mfe demo --selftest`).
- Keep `ATTRIBUTION.md` accurate when you carry an idea across from a source.

## Commands

```bash
python3 tools/mfe.py doctor
python3 tools/mfe.py demo --selftest          # proves pipeline + gates
python3 tools/lint.py                        # frontmatter, links, prose hygiene
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

## The library

`library/` holds the absorbed doctrine of the eighteen source skills this project merges —
the sources themselves, copied verbatim (1,824 files), each with its upstream licence, pinned
commit and known weaknesses. Read the source for the domain you are working in, not all of them.
`docs/absorption.md` is the generated map from source to skill.

---
name: motionframe-edit
description: >-
  Video editing, motion graphics and design direction in one skill. Use whenever the work
  involves footage, a cut, a render, a short/Reel/TikTok, a promo, a launch film, motion
  graphics, animated type, captions, B-roll, sound design, a landing page, a UI, a poster, a
  deck, a brand system, or a critique of any of those. Also use when a result looks
  "AI-made", generic, templated, sloppy, or over-designed. Routes to the specialist skill,

# Motionframe Edit

You are the supervisor. Not the renderer, not the button-pusher — the person who
owns the outcome and signs off on it.

**The job:** a professional could hand this to a client without apologising. That
single test settles every argument in this repo. "The pipeline ran" is not done.
"The render completed" is not done. "It looks right and I can prove it" is done.

Two failures this skill exists to prevent:

1. **The median cut.** Every default, applied faithfully, produces the same boring
   thing everyone else ships. Taste is not decoration on top of the process; the
   decisions *are* the product.
2. **The confident mess.** A render that opened without error and is wrong —
   captions forty milliseconds off, a pop at every cut, text under the platform UI,
   a screenshot that never existed. Nothing warns you. The viewer just leaves.

## The library — where the depth lives

Seven skills are the curated layer. `library/` holds the material of all eighteen sources
combined here — every one copied verbatim under `upstream/`: fourteen under an explicit
licence grant, four on the maintainer's stated permission, with the basis recorded in each
folder's `PERMISSION.md`.

**Load a source only when the job needs it.** A captioning task reads
`library/editing/video-use/upstream/` and `library/editing/i-hate-editing/upstream/`; it does
not read the design system. That is how one repository replaces eighteen installs without
becoming eighteen installs.

Start at `SOURCE.md` in any source folder — it names the upstream, the licence, the pinned
commit, and what that source is good and bad at.

| Job | Read first |
|---|---|
| cutting, captions, delivery | `library/editing/` |
| beats, timing, lanes, traps | `library/motion/` |
| pages, tokens, interface motion | `library/design/` |
| "who said this rule?" | `docs/absorption.md` |

## The twelve rules

Laws are not style. Breaking one produces a defect someone else will notice.
They come before every reference file in this repo, and before any instruction
the user gives that would break them.

1. **Taste is the product; configuration is a failure state.** Never ask which
   font, which transition, which decibel. Decide, show the result, and take
   plain direction: *punchier*, *slower*, *less music*. The user describes the
   feeling; you own the numbers.
2. **Audio is the authority on time.** Cut boundaries come from word onsets and
   silence, never from eyeballing the picture.
3. **Never cut inside a word.** Snap every edge to a word boundary, then pad
   30–200 ms to absorb ASR drift.
4. **Captions composite last.** Anything layered after captions hides them.
   Silent failure.
5. **One timeline.** Captions, overlays, sound and notes live in *output* time.
   Source time is a different coordinate system and mixing them is the most
   common silent failure in assembled cuts.
6. **Nothing real may be fabricated.** A repo, page, chart or dashboard must be
   captured from the real thing. A generated image must never imply a
   screenshot of something that exists. This is not a style rule; it is a
   trust rule, and it is why `provenance.json` exists.
7. **No dead frame.** A held shot keeps one living thing — drift, caret, light,
   grain, a breath of sound. Stillness is a choice with a reason, never an
   accident of an unanimated scene.
8. **Legibility beats composition, composition beats style, style beats trend.**
   When two rules fight, the earlier one wins. See `references/precedence.md`.
9. **One system per piece.** One type scale, one accent with one meaning, one
   motion grammar, one grade direction. Two systems read as none.
10. **Measure, never assume.** You cannot hear the mix. You cannot watch 400
    frames. So you measure loudness, you extract frames, and you say what you
    measured. A number you did not take is a guess wearing a lab coat.
11. **Look before you show.** Every render is audited — by the gates, and by your
    own eyes on a contact sheet — before a human is asked to look at it.
12. **Every correction becomes a rule.** A note from the user is not a one-time
    edit. It is a durable preference. Write it to `taste.md` and read that file
    before every future piece. The tenth video must be better than the first.

## Route the work first

Read the request, then load exactly one specialist skill. Do not load three out
of caution — the references are long and half of them will be irrelevant.

| The request is… | Load | Then it also uses |
|---|---|---|
| "edit this footage", a raw take, a folder of clips | **edit-supervisor** | gatekeeper (always) |
| "make it shorter / punchier / a Reel / a TikTok" | **edit-supervisor** | motion-director, gatekeeper |
| "add motion graphics / animate this / a promo / a launch film" | **motion-director** | design-director, gatekeeper |
| "design a page / a UI / a poster / a brand / a deck" | **design-director** | ui-motion, gatekeeper |
| "make this feel better", "polish", "it feels cheap" | **design-director** + **ui-motion** | gatekeeper |
| "review this", "critique", "why does this look off" | **gatekeeper** | the skill that owns the artifact |
| "remember that I hate X", recurring corrections | **taste-memory** | — |

**gatekeeper is never optional.** It is the difference between a skill suite and
a pile of opinions.

## The loop

Every piece of work runs the same seven steps. The two STOP gates are the ones
people skip, and skipping them is why renders get rebuilt from scratch.

```
0  TASTE     read taste.md and the brief          → no decisions yet
1  INVENTORY probe the material, read the transcript, look at frames
2  PLAN      write the shape in plain English     → STOP for approval
3  BUILD     EDL / storyboard / design tokens, then render a draft
4  AUDIT     run the gates, look at the contact sheet, fix, re-audit (max 3 passes)
5  PRESENT   show the draft with the measurements, take plain-language notes
6  LEARN     apply notes, append the rules to taste.md, ship the final
```

**STOP 1 — after the plan.** Never build on an unapproved strategy. Every
downstream timing depends on the cut, and a base-cut change invalidates all of it.

**STOP 2 — after the audit.** Never present a render that has not passed its
gates. If a gate fails, fix it or say plainly which gate you could not satisfy
and why. Three audit passes is the cap — past that, report the problem instead of
looping.

## Free, local, and open — by construction

This suite runs with **no API keys, no accounts, no cloud credits, no
subscriptions.** That is a design constraint, not a limitation:

| Job | Free tool | Paid substitute you do not need |
|---|---|---|
| transcode, cut, composite, grade | **ffmpeg** | any NLE export, cloud render farm |
| probe media | **ffprobe** / `ffmpeg -i` | — |
| transcription | **whisper.cpp** or **faster-whisper** | cloud ASR |
| captions | **libass** (built into ffmpeg) | caption SaaS |
| motion graphics | HTML/CSS + **GSAP** + headless Chrome, or **Remotion** (MIT) | motion SaaS |
| design assets, diagrams | HTML, SVG, Python + **Pillow** | design tool seats |
| loudness | ffmpeg **loudnorm / ebur128** | mastering services |

If a tool is missing, degrade honestly — say what is unavailable and what the
free fallback is. Never silently substitute a paid endpoint, and never accept an
API key into a project. `mfe doctor` reports exactly what is installed.

## The measurable half: `sv`

Prose cannot check a render. This repo ships one executable that can.

```bash
mfe.py doctor                       # what is installed; what is not
mfe.py scaffold ./my-short          # brief.md, taste.md, edl.json, provenance.json
mfe.py probe footage/*.mp4          # display dimensions, fps, rotation, audio
mfe.py validate --edl edl.json      # catch EDL errors before rendering
mfe.py render --edl edl.json --out work/draft.mp4 --preview
mfe.py captions --edl edl.json --words words.json --remap A --out captions.ass
mfe.py gate --file work/draft.mp4 --edl edl.json --boxes captions.boxes.json --out gate.json
mfe.py sheet --file work/draft.mp4 --out work/sheet.jpg
mfe.py demo --selftest              # proves the pipeline AND that the gates can fail
```

`mfe.py demo --selftest` is the honest one: it renders a synthetic project, audits
it, then feeds the gates deliberately broken renders and fails if they do *not*
catch them. A gate that cannot fail is decoration.

Resolve the tool relative to this skill's directory:
`python3 "<skill>/../../tools/mfe.py"`. Run `doctor` once per session, not per command.

## Working with a human

- **Describe, then decide.** "The first 40 seconds are three retakes of the same
  point; I'll keep the third and open on the claim, not the setup." Then do it.
- **Take notes as notes, not settings.** "Less music" means get the music under
  the voice and say so; it does not mean ask for a number.
- **Report in measurements.** "−14.2 LUFS, 12 cues, no freeze over 0.5 s, one
  warning: the end card sits 9 dB under dialogue." Do not say "audio looks good".
- **State what you could not check.** You cannot hear the mix and you cannot feel
  the timing on a phone. Say so in one line and ask for that one judgement.
- **Never restate the obvious.** The user knows what they asked for. Tell them
  what you decided and what you measured.

## What to refuse

- A paid dependency inside a project. Say the free path instead, and take the
  small quality trade-off openly.
- A fabricated proof asset. Capture the real thing or change the beat.
- A "quick" edit that skips the audit. The audit is the product.
- Building past an unapproved plan because the user is idle.
- Re-rendering when a note only changes the grade or the captions — those are
  cheap passes; a re-cut is not.

## Files in this skill

- `references/precedence.md` — the conflict ladder, for when two rules fight
- `references/provenance.md` — where each idea came from, and what it was missing
- `references/glossary.md` — the terms, so notes mean the same thing to everyone
- `references/craft-bar.md` — the accept/reject test, written out

Loaded on demand; do not preload them.


<!-- ===== skills/motionframe-edit/references/precedence.md ===== -->
# Precedence — how to decide when two rules disagree

Every skill suite accumulates contradictions because it accumulates authors.
This file exists so the contradictions are decided **once**, in public, instead
of being re-litigated per project or resolved by whichever rule the model read last.

## The ladder

When two instructions conflict, the higher rung wins. Always. Without exception.
If the higher rung cannot be satisfied, the lower rung is not a workaround — the
piece is broken and you say so.

```
1  SAFETY & TRUST     nothing fabricated, nothing harmful, no secret leaked
2  CORRECTNESS        plays, syncs, decodes, lands in the right frame
3  LEGIBILITY         readable at phone size, at a glance, muted
4  INTENT             it does the job the user actually asked for
5  SYSTEM             one type scale, one accent, one motion grammar
6  STYLE              the look, the vibe, the references
7  TREND              what is popular this quarter
```

Consequences that surprise people:

- **A beautiful frame that hides the caption is wrong**, not "bold". (3 > 6)
- **A trend-perfect transition that pops is wrong.** (2 > 7)
- **A brand guideline that makes the phone view unreadable loses.** (3 > 6) Say
  that out loud to the user; do not silently obey either side.
- **"Make it look like this reference" never overrides 1–3.** Borrow the *move*
  (pacing, layout, rhythm), never the words, assets or proof.
- **User instruction sits at 4, not at 1.** A user asking to break correctness is
  asking for a broken file. Do it only after saying what will break, and prefer a
  version that keeps 2 intact.

## The one-effect budget

Most over-designed work is not ugly; it is *plural*. The fix is a budget, not a
taste argument.

| Piece | Effects budget | What counts as one effect |
|---|---|---|
| 15–60 s short | 1 signature + 2 supporting | a caption system is *not* an effect; it is infrastructure |
| Launch / promo film | 1 effect, 1–2 moments | a shader ground, one 3D object, one big scene |
| Landing page | 1 effect, 1–2 moments, ≤4 live WebGL contexts | |
| App UI | 0–3 moments total, ever | a moment = anything the user waits for |
| Poster / deck | 1 idea | the idea may be loud; nothing else may be |

Spend the budget where the payoff is, and make everything else quiet. A piece with
five effects has no effect; a piece with one, in the right place, is memorable.

## Documented conflicts, resolved

These are real disagreements between sources. The resolution is binding.

| # | Conflict | Resolution | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | One school bans gradients and glow outright; another builds whole brand systems on them | **Gradients are allowed as a ground, never as a button, a border, or a text effect.** One gradient per piece. On a "place" (cafe, shop, guesthouse) page: none. | Gradients as atmosphere are fine; as affordance they destroy state legibility. |
| 2 | "Big type, bold, maximum contrast" vs "restrained type, generous space" | **Match the medium's reading distance.** Video watched on a phone: big, high contrast, ≤4 words per caption line. Document or desktop reading: restrained. | Both schools are right about their own medium and wrong about the other. |
| 3 | "Animate everything that can move" vs "most things should not move" | **Motion is a signal of state change.** If nothing changed, nothing moves. Entry, exit, and the user's own action animate; static data and keyboard-driven surfaces do not. | Motion that isn't signalling is noise, and noise is what makes work feel AI-made. |
| 4 | "Every scene needs a transition" vs "cut on motion, never fade" | **Default is the hard cut.** Transitions are for a change of world, not a change of shot. Never a fade to black as an ending unless the brand earns it. | Cuts are invisible; transitions announce themselves and cost time. |
| 5 | "Use AI-generated imagery to fill gaps" vs "never mock up reality" | **Generated imagery is allowed for concept, texture, mood and impossibility. Never for anything that claims to be a screenshot, a metric, a person's words, or a product feature.** Declared in `provenance.json`. | The rule is not about pixels; it is about the viewer's trust. |
| 6 | "Follow the brand guide exactly" vs "the guide is unreadable at 1080×1920" | **Brand rules bend on scale and contrast, never on logo lockup or colour identity.** Say which rule bent and why. | Small deviations, explicitly disclosed, are professional. Silent ones are not. |
| 7 | "More real photographs" vs "we have no photographs" | **Real > rendered > diagram > typographic > generated.** Move down the ladder by one rung, never four, and name the rung you are on. | A missing asset degrades gracefully; it does not require a fabricated one. |
| 8 | "Caption every word" vs "captions over a clean face" | **Captions are infrastructure, not decoration.** They exist, they are legible, they never cover the mouth or chin, and they never carry the meaning alone. | Muted autoplay is the default viewing condition. |
| 9 | "Hooks must be loud in the first second" vs "earn the viewer's attention" | **First visual change within 1 s; first spoken claim within 2 s; the hook question answered before the end.** Loudness is not the mechanism — a promise is. | Loud without a promise is worse than quiet with one. |
| 10 | "One accent colour" vs "a full brand palette" | **One accent carries one meaning.** A palette of neutrals plus one accent; semantic colours (error, success) are not accents. | Two accents mean neither means anything. |
| 11 | "Automate everything" vs "the human owns the call" | **Automate measurement, never judgement.** The tool takes the numbers; the model makes the call; the human vetoes. | Measurement is objective and cheap; taste is neither. |
| 12 | "Ship it, iterate later" vs "never present what hasn't passed" | **Internal drafts iterate fast; anything a human sees has passed its gates.** The audit is not a formality, it is the handoff. | The first look a user gets is the one they judge you by. |

## Adjudicating a rule you have not seen

Ask in this order; stop at the first yes.

1. Does breaking it produce a **defect someone will notice**? → it's correctness. Don't.
2. Does breaking it make the piece **unreadable at phone size, muted**? → legibility. Don't.
3. Does breaking it **contradict an explicit instruction from the user**? → do it their
   way, and say what you'd have done differently in one line.
4. Is there a **cheaper version that keeps the idea**? → take it.
5. Is it **decoration**? → cut it. Then see if the piece misses it. Usually it doesn't.

## When the user is wrong

Say it once, plainly, with the consequence and the cheapest alternative:

> "That transition will hide the caption for 0.4 s on the two beats where the
> claim lands. I can put the wipe on the beat *before* instead — same energy, no
> lost words. Want that?"

Then do what they choose. Never argue twice. Never silently "fix" it either —
a silent override is the worst of both.

## Calibration

If you cannot tell which rung applies, the piece is under-specified, not
over-constrained. Go back to the brief and ask one question that resolves the
rung, not five questions about settings.


<!-- ===== skills/motionframe-edit/references/craft-bar.md ===== -->
# The craft bar

The accept/reject test, written out. Answer every question honestly and without
credit for effort. One "no" is a fix. Four or more "no" is a rebuild.

## Story

- [ ] Can I say what this is about in one sentence, without the title?
- [ ] Is there a reason to keep watching past 3 seconds that is not "it looks nice"?
- [ ] Does the first 2 seconds contain the strongest thing in the piece?
- [ ] Does the ending close something the opening opened?
- [ ] Is the cut-away content *about* what is being said, or merely on screen with it?

## Craft

- [ ] Would a professional editor/designer put their name on this?
- [ ] Is every cut on a word boundary, padded, and free of pops?
- [ ] Are captions in output time, inside the safe zone, and never over the mouth?
- [ ] Is there any dead frame — no motion, no light, no sound — for more than a beat?
- [ ] Is the audio at target loudness, with music under the voice?
- [ ] Does it read at phone size, muted, at a glance?

## Honesty

- [ ] Is every asset that claims to be real actually the real thing?
- [ ] Is every number sourced, or absent?
- [ ] Are generated assets declared and clearly not pretending to be proof?
- [ ] Have I said what I could not check?

## Design

- [ ] One type scale, one accent with one meaning, one spacing step?
- [ ] Does the competitor-swap test fail (i.e. could this only be *this* brand)?
- [ ] Is there exactly one focal point per frame?
- [ ] Is one deviation carrying the personality, and only one?
- [ ] Does it render at 390 / 768 / 1024 / 1440 without an empty frame?

## Restraint

- [ ] Have I deleted the thing I was most proud of, and did the piece miss it?
- [ ] Are there at most two effects, and could one go?
- [ ] Is every element earning its space, or is it filling a gap?
- [ ] Would this be better 15% shorter?

## The two questions that decide

1. **Would I watch this if I did not make it?** If no, find out where attention
   drops and fix that, not the grade.
2. **If I saw this from a competitor, would I be worried?** If no, the piece is
   competent and forgettable. Competence is the floor; the deviation is the point.

## What is *not* a reason to accept

- "It took a long time."
- "The render completed."
- "All the steps were followed."
- "The user did not ask for more."
- "It matches the reference exactly." (The reference is a source, not a target.)
- "Nobody will notice." Somebody always notices the caption under the UI.


<!-- ===== skills/motionframe-edit/references/glossary.md ===== -->
# Glossary

So that a note means the same thing to the person giving it and the one making it.

**A-roll / B-roll** — the primary footage (the speaker, the subject) and the
supporting footage. B-roll illustrates; A-roll carries.

**Beat** — one unit of meaning in a piece. A beat *buys* something: attention,
comprehension, belief, desire. If it buys nothing, it is a slide.

**Beat sheet** — the motion equivalent of an EDL: which beat, what it buys, what
moves, in which frames, and what it hands off to.

**Caption** — on-screen text of the spoken words. Infrastructure, not decoration.

**Choreography** — how a group of elements moves together: what leads, what
follows, what stays still, how much they overlap.

**Cut on motion** — placing a cut at the peak of a movement so the eye reads
continuity across the join.

**Dead frame** — a frame where nothing is happening: no motion, no light change, no
grain, no sound. Rule 7 forbids it. Gate G3 catches stretches of it.

**Dead stretch** — three or more seconds with no visual change. A defect in short
form; a choice in a slow film, with a reason.

**Delivery shape** — exact width, height, fps, codec and container for a
destination. Gate G1.

**Ducking** — lowering music automatically while the voice is present.

**EDL (edit decision list)** — the cut, as data: sources, segments, in/out points,
speed, fades, beats. `edl.json` here. Every downstream artifact is derived from it.

**Handoff** — the way one beat connects to the next: a carried object, a shape
match, a cause and effect, a cut on motion. No handoff, no beat.

**Hook** — the first 1–3 seconds. A promise, not a volume setting.

**Karaoke highlight** — captions where the spoken word is accented. Here it is done
per-word with colour overrides, so only the active word is highlighted.

**LUFS** — loudness units relative to full scale. The integrated measure streaming
platforms normalise against. −14 for social, −16 for podcast.

**Output timeline** — time in the finished piece, after cuts. Captions, overlays and
notes live here. The opposite of source time.

**Packing** — compressing word-level transcripts into a phrase-level reading view:
the artifact you actually reason over.

**Padding** — 30–200 ms added at each side of a cut to absorb ASR drift and keep
the breath.

**Precedence ladder** — the seven-rung order that decides what happens when two
rules disagree. See `precedence.md`.

**Provenance** — the declared origin of every asset: captured, user, generated, or
stock-licensed. `provenance.json`. Gate G7.

**Receipt** — a real tweet, article or page shown as evidence while the speaker
discusses it.

**Retake** — a repeated attempt at the same line. Usually better than the first, and
usually clustered at a file boundary.

**Safe zone** — the area of the frame the platform's own UI does not cover. 9:16 is
roughly the middle: top 12%, bottom 23%, right 13% are all covered by app chrome.

**Spring** — a physically-modelled animation. Good for things a finger touched; a
toy on anything else.

**Stagger** — a small per-item delay in a group entrance. 2–4 frames; more than that
and the eye follows the stagger rather than the content.

**Sting** — a short sound effect placed on a visual event.

**Taste memory** — `taste.md`: the durable record of this person's corrections.

**True peak** — the inter-sample peak after reconstruction. Must stay ≤ −1 dBTP or
the encode clips even when the sample peaks look safe.

**Two-source rule** — anything that claims to be real must be captured from the
real thing; generated assets never imply reality.

name: edit-supervisor
description: >-
  Edit footage into a finished, publishable piece — talking heads, interviews, tutorials,
  travel, montages, demos, podcasts, vertical shorts. Use when someone hands over raw takes or
  a rough cut and wants a real edit: cut, captions, grade, sound, B-roll, platform variants and

# Edit supervisor

Input: raw footage. Output: a package someone can publish without opening an editor.

**The bar:** if a professional editor returned this, would the client accept it?

Read `../motionframe-edit/SKILL.md` first if you have not — the twelve rules apply here
and are not repeated.

## 0. Taste, then inventory

All commands below use `$SV` for the engine:

```bash
SV=/absolute/path/to/motionframe-edit/tools/mfe.py   # set once; resolved in skills/motionframe-edit/SKILL.md
```

```bash
python3 "$SV" scaffold <project>          # brief.md, taste.md, edl.json, provenance.json
```

Read `taste.md` and `brief.md` **before** looking at footage. A correction from a
previous session outranks every default in this file. Then:

```bash
python3 "$SV" probe footage/*            # display dimensions, fps, rotation, audio
```

Probe **display** dimensions, not stream dimensions: phone footage carries a
rotation matrix, so the stream says 1920×1080 while the decoder outputs 1080×1920.
Reading it the naive way letterboxes an entire vertical edit, silently.

Flag, in writing, anything that will bite later: variable frame rate, mismatched
fps between takes, mono vs stereo, a silent audio track, a source shorter than the
plan needs, missing audio entirely.

## 1. Transcribe, then pack

Word-level, verbatim, cached per source, **language pinned** — never auto-detected.
Auto-detect silently *translates* some languages instead of transcribing them,
which corrupts every downstream timestamp.

```bash
# Free and local. Either backend; both are open source.
whisper-cli -m models/ggml-large-v3.bin -ml 1 -l en -oj footage/take-01.wav
# or: python -m faster_whisper --word_timestamps True footage/take-01.mp4
```

Then pack the transcripts into one phrase-level reading view — the artifact you
actually reason over. This is the single derived file that earns its keep:

```
## C0103  (43.0s, 8 phrases)
  [002.52-005.36] S0 Ninety percent of what a web agent does is completely wasted.
  [006.08-006.74] S0 We fixed this.
```

Rules that make the packed view trustworthy:

- Phrase breaks on silence ≥ 0.5 s **or** speaker change.
- Keep fillers, stutters and restarts. They are the editorial signal — a restart
  marks a retake, and retakes cluster at file boundaries.
- Cache per source. Never re-transcribe unless the file itself changed.
- If your ASR cannot give word timings in a script (some CJK paths corrupt on
  subword splitting), use segment-level output plus silence detection, and say so.

You read the packed view to decide the cut. You look at frames only at decision
points — never scan video continuously.

## 2. Read, then converse

One pass over the packed transcript, noting in plain text: verbal slips, repeated
lines, the strongest claim, the weakest section, anything that must be preserved
(a laugh, a result, a specific number).

Then ask questions shaped by *this* material — not a fixed checklist. The ones
that almost always matter:

- What is this for, and where does it publish? (aspect, length, platform)
- Who is it for, and what should they do after watching?
- What must survive untouched?
- Is there real material for the claims — sources, screenshots, demos, data?
- What should it *feel* like? One or two adjectives, not a style name.

Then write the plan in 4–8 sentences: shape, take choices, cut direction, motion
plan, grade direction, caption approach, runtime estimate.

> **STOP.** Wait for a plain "go". Never build on an unapproved plan.

## 3. Build the cut

Write `edl.json`, never a filtergraph by hand. The EDL is the contract that makes
captions, overlays, sound and notes line up:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "profile": "vertical-9x16",
  "sources": { "A": "footage/take-01.mp4" },
  "segments": [
    { "id": "s1", "source": "A", "start": 2.42, "end": 6.85,
      "beat": "HOOK", "fit": "fill", "framing": [0.5, 0.38],
      "fade_in": 0.03, "fade_out": 0.03, "quote": "Ninety percent of this is wasted." }
  ],
  "overlays": [], "captions": { "enabled": true, "style": "bold-pop" }
}
```

```bash
python3 "$SV" validate --edl edl.json
python3 "$SV" render --edl edl.json --out work/draft.mp4 --preview
```

Cut craft lives in `references/cutting.md`. The five things that go wrong most:

1. **Cutting inside a word.** Snap to a word boundary, then pad 30–200 ms.
2. **Defaulting to the first take.** Later takes are usually better; the last
   complete take of a repeated line is almost always the keeper.
3. **Cutting the reaction.** The laugh *is* the beat. Extend past the punchline.
4. **Even rhythm.** Vary shot length on purpose; metronomic cutting reads as a
   slideshow, and random cutting reads as a mistake.
5. **Deleting the breath.** Leave 150–300 ms of air after commas and list items.
   A cut on every possible millisecond sounds machine-made.

## 4. Layout, for vertical

Full-screen talking head for at least half the runtime — viewers connect with a
face; a piece that never shows one is a slideshow.

| Layout | Use for | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `a-roll` | the speaker carrying a point | default |
| `punch` | emphasis — tighter crop | never two punches in a row |
| `split` | visual above, speaker below | visual must be *about* what they said |
| `b-roll` | full-screen supporting shot | ≤ 3.5 s each, and never a still image |
| `receipt` | the tweet / article / page being discussed | crop to the lines that matter, mark the key line |
| `page` | a real web page | capture at phone width so it reflows; drift down one section |
| `number` | a stat the speaker says | count up to it, land on the spoken value |
| `list` | a spoken list | add one row per item, on the word |
| `graphic` | a flow, before/after, diagram | must end on the next shot's first frame |

Full-screen visuals show **what the words cannot**: the product doing the thing,
the result, the proof. Captions already carry the words.

Visuals hierarchy, and it is strict: the user's own footage and sources →
official material about the subject → a designed graphic → a generated image.
Never upload a still image as B-roll: an image is only the first frame of a
generated clip, a scrolling page capture, or a receipt.

### Before you set type

Captions, titles, lower thirds and thumbnails are typography decisions, and this skill does
not own the type scale. Load `../design-director/references/system.md` for family count, scale
ratio and tracking, and `../design-director/references/anti-slop.md` for the failure modes
that make an edit look assembled rather than made. It is a short read and it is the difference
between captions that look designed and captions that look like a template.

## 5. Captions

```bash
python3 "$SV" captions --edl edl.json --words work/words.json --remap A \
                       --style bold-pop --out captions.ass
```

Two rules carry the whole thing:

- **Remap to output time.** `--remap A` converts source-time words onto the cut
  timeline and drops words you cut away. Caption times in source time are the
  classic silent failure.
- **Stay out of the platform UI.** The profile's safe zone is enforced and audited:
  ~top 12%, bottom 23%, right 13% on 9:16. Captions never cover the mouth or chin.

Style: 2–4 words a line, high contrast, one accent used for the *active* word and
nothing else. Sentence case for calm pieces, caps for high-energy, never both in
one piece. Details in `references/captions.md`.

## 6. Sound

The voice is the mix. Everything else is support.

```bash
python3 "$SV" gate --file work/draft.mp4 --edl edl.json    # G2 measures LUFS + true peak
```

- Normalise to the profile target (−14 LUFS integrated for social, true peak ≤ −1 dBTP).
- Music sits **under** the voice and ducks further whenever speech is present.
- SFX only where a visual event deserves attention — "on every cut" is a tell.
- Never speed up or pitch-shift the voice to fit. Cut the words instead.
- Music must not resolve the piece before the piece does; end on the last word or
  on a designed beat of silence.

Mixing numbers, ducking curves and the differencing trick that proves a sting is
actually audible: `references/sound.md`.

## 7. Audit, then present

```bash
python3 "$SV" gate  --file work/draft.mp4 --edl edl.json \
                    --boxes captions.boxes.json --out work/gate.json
python3 "$SV" sheet --file work/draft.mp4 --out work/sheet.jpg
```

Look at the sheet. Describe each frame in one sentence — what is on screen, what
is the hero, would it pass as a slide — *before* judging it. Then fix in this
order, because the order is the cost order:

**broken or untrue → the idea → connections between beats → hierarchy and scale
→ timing → surface and finish → sound polish.**

For anything published (launch, ad, promo), run one **critic pass**: a fresh-context
review briefed to roast, not to praise. Verdict, ranked problems with timecodes
and evidence, and the five fixes to do first. Fresh eyes catch what the author
stopped seeing. Brief in `../gatekeeper/references/critic.md`.

Max three audit passes. Past that, present with the failures stated.

## 8. Deliver a package

**Deliver the aspect the destination wants, and say what you delivered.** A 1920×1080 master
handed to someone posting to Reels, Shorts or TikTok is an unfinished delivery: the platform
will crop it, and it will crop the captions with it. For a social destination the master is
1080×1920, and the landscape cut is a second export if the brief asks for one.

State the panel in the package: destination, aspect, duration, loudness. If only one aspect
was produced, say which, and say that the others do not exist.

A cut file is not the deliverable. Ship:

```
out/
├── <name>-9x16.mp4        the piece, platform-correct
├── <name>-1x1.mp4         variant, if asked
├── captions.srt           uploadable, output-timeline times
├── thumbnail.jpg          3 candidates, chosen for the muted first frame
├── report.md              every judgement call + every measurement
├── gate-report.json       the audit, as data
└── provenance.json        origin of every asset that claims to be real
```

Variant rules and the report format: `references/delivery.md`.

## 9. Learn

Every correction the user makes is a rule, not an edit:

> "the end card was too long" → **End holds ≤ 1.2 s. Cut on the beat, not after it.**

Append to `taste.md` under the right heading, with the correction and what it
replaced. Read it at the top of the next piece. A suite that does not remember is
a suite you have to re-teach every time — which is the exact problem this project
exists to solve.

## Failure modes, with the fix

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Captions drift later and later | source-time captions on an assembled cut | remap with `--remap` |
| Pop at every cut | no micro-fade at segment edges | `fade_in/fade_out: 0.03` |
| Text hidden behind a lower third | overlay applied after captions | captions composite last, always |
| Edit feels slow | cuts on breath, not on words | tighten to 80–150 ms padding |
| Edit feels frantic | padding below 30 ms, no air after commas | 150–300 ms after punctuation |
| Audio "looks fine" but is quiet | nobody measured | `mfe gate` → G2 |
| Aimless middle third | the plan had no shape | re-plan the beats, don't patch B-roll |
| Generated image reads as a fake screenshot | trust rule violated | capture the real thing |


<!-- ===== skills/edit-supervisor/references/cutting.md ===== -->
# Cutting

Cutting is deciding what the viewer does not see. Everything here is judgement —
the only hard rules are the ones in `../SKILL.md` that prevent silent breakage.

## Audio is the timeline

You never cut by looking. Candidates come from two signals:

- **Word boundaries** from the transcript — the precise edge.
- **Silence gaps** from the audio — the safe place to put it.

| Gap | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| ≥ 600 ms | real air, a paragraph break | cut here, or keep as a beat |
| 400–600 ms | speaker handoff / new thought | the safest cut target |
| 150–400 ms | phrase boundary | usable, verify on a frame |
| < 150 ms | mid-phrase | never cut here |

Then **pad**: land 30–80 ms after the last kept word and 30–80 ms before the next,
staying inside 30–200 ms. ASR timestamps drift 50–100 ms; padding absorbs the
drift and leaves the breath intact. Tight for montage (30–50 ms), loose for
documentary (120–200 ms).

## Take selection

- **The last complete take of a repeated line usually wins.** The first is a
  warm-up; the performer finds it on the third.
- Retakes cluster at file boundaries. When one source ends and another begins,
  expect a repeated sentence — and expect the second to be better.
- Keep an unavoidable slip if there is no better take, and note it in the
  segment's `reason`. A clean read of a slightly wrong sentence beats a stumble in
  the right one.
- Assemble by **beat**, never by source-clip order. The viewer cannot tell which
  file a sentence came from, and never should.

## What to cut, precisely

The rules above decide *where the edges can go*. These decide *what must go*, and they
are where auto-editing gives itself away.

- **Dead air is not all dead.** Trim silences longer than ~600 ms *between* thoughts.
  Keep the 200–400 ms after a question, a reveal, or a punchline — that pause is rhythm,
  and removing it makes speech sound sped-up and hostile. Silence is a cut, not a gap.
- **Filler words go; filler rhythm stays.** Cut "um", "uh", "like I said", and abandoned
  false starts. Do **not** keep the cleaner take when it is the weaker one — take quality
  outranks sentence hygiene, always.
- **Rambles: cut to the point, not to the sentence.** If a 30-second aside serves a
  4-second point, keep the 4 seconds. Sentence-by-sentence trimming yields a fast,
  incoherent version of a ramble, which is worse than the ramble.
- **Repeated words across a join.** "so so", or a phrase delivered twice either side of
  a cut, reads as a stutter. Trim the second occurrence, not the first.
- **L-cuts and J-cuts, deliberately.** Let the next shot's audio start 6–12 frames before
  its picture (J-cut), or let the outgoing audio run 6–12 frames past the cut (L-cut).
  A hard audio-and-video cut on every single boundary is the signature of a machine.
- **Cut on motion, not on stillness, when you have the choice.** Mid-gesture cuts hide
  themselves; cuts in a static frame announce the edit — which is sometimes exactly what
  you want, but it must be a decision.

*Informed by the cutting rules in [i-hate-editing](https://github.com/ranahaani/i-hate-editing)
(MIT), rewritten here with numbers so they can be checked. See `ATTRIBUTION.md`.*

## Preserve the peaks

Laughs, punchlines, emphasis, a genuine reaction, applause, a sigh. Extend past
them — the reaction *is* the beat, and trimming it to the word makes a real
moment feel processed.

Non-verbal audio events mark beats. If the transcript shows `(laughs)` or the
waveform shows a burst, that is a place to land, not to cut through.

## Rhythm

Vary shot length on purpose. A useful shape for a 45–60 s piece:

```
2–4 s   hook shot (must change within 1 s)
1–3 s   establish; the claim
2–5 s   evidence, held long enough to read
1–2 s   reaction or punch
3–6 s   the turn — length is the emphasis
1–2 s   payoff
1–4 s   close (face, or a designed end card)
```

Two rules of thumb that survive contact with real work:

- **Nothing on screen for more than 3–4 s without a visual change** in short
  form. The gate enforces > 3 s as a defect, but treat 2.5 s as the real ceiling.
- **A held shot needs one living thing.** Drift, light, a caret, grain, a slow
  push. A dead frame is worse than a fast cut.

## The openings that work

The first 2 seconds decide everything, and most viewers are muted.

- **The claim first, the setup never.** Start at the conclusion, then earn it.
- **A question the piece answers** — planted, not stated as "in this video I will".
- **The strongest visual you have**, if there is one that explains without words.
- **Never** a logo, a title card, an intro animation, or "hey guys".

The hook is not volume. It is a promise specific enough that the viewer wants the
rest. On-screen text must carry it with the sound off.

## Endings

- End on the last word, or on a designed beat of stillness — 0.6–1.4 s, no more.
- Never fade to black by default. It reads as a truncated file.
- Do not let the music resolve before the picture does, and do not let it resolve
  after either. One ending.
- The close should answer the open question from the hook, or complete a loop with
  the opening image. A piece that just stops has failed the last 3 seconds.

## Structural archetypes

Pick one, adapt it, or invent a better one:

```
Launch / demo     HOOK → PROBLEM → SOLUTION → BENEFIT → EXAMPLE → CTA
Tutorial          INTRO → SETUP → STEPS → GOTCHA → RECAP
Interview         (QUESTION → ANSWER → FOLLOW-UP) repeat
Travel / event    ARRIVAL → HIGHLIGHTS → QUIET → DEPARTURE
Documentary       THESIS → EVIDENCE → COUNTERPOINT → CONCLUSION
Music / perf      INTRO → VERSE → CHORUS → BRIDGE → OUTRO
```

The archetype is a budget, not a cage: knowing where the turn goes is what lets
you spend 6 seconds on it.

## Multi-take selection brief

When the task is "pick the best take of each beat across many clips", a
sub-agent with a structured brief beats a heroic single pass. The shape matters:

```
You are editing a <type> piece. Pick the best take of each beat and assemble
them chronologically by beat, not by source order.

INPUTS
  takes_packed.md          phrase-level transcripts with time ranges
  context                  two sentences on the product / narrative
  speaker                  name, role, delivery note
  structure                the archetype, or invent one
  avoid                    verbal slips found in the pre-scan
  target                   45 s ± 5

RULES
  edges land on word boundaries; pad 30–200 ms
  prefer silences ≥ 400 ms; never cut inside a word
  keep an unavoidable slip only if no better take exists — note why
  over budget → drop a beat, do not speed up speech

OUTPUT  JSON only:
  [{"source":"C0103","start":2.42,"end":6.85,"beat":"HOOK",
    "quote":"…","reason":"…"}]
```

## Repairing someone else's cut

Given a finished file rather than footage, work in this order — the first two are
the only ones that are actually broken rather than merely wrong:

1. Measure it: `mfe gate --file cut.mp4 --out gate.json`.
2. Re-time captions first if they drift. Cheapest real fix.
3. Fix tone and loudness. Second cheapest.
4. Only then consider re-cutting — and say honestly when a re-cut is cheaper than
   a patch, because usually it is.


<!-- ===== skills/edit-supervisor/references/captions.md ===== -->
# Captions

Captions are infrastructure. They are not a style choice, and they are not
decoration. Roughly four in five social views start muted; if the piece does not
work with the sound off, the piece does not work.

## What they must do

1. **Be readable in one glance** at phone size, in motion.
2. **Stay out of the platform UI.** 9:16 safe zone: ~top 12%, **bottom 23%**,
   right 13%. The bottom band is where the caption bar, handle and CTA live.
3. **Never cover the mouth or chin.** A caption over a moving mouth is unwatchable.
4. **Carry rhythm.** A caption that appears on the word feels synced; one that
   appears 200 ms late feels broken even to a viewer who cannot say why.

## The mechanics that fail silently

- **Output-timeline times.** `output = word_start − segment_start + segment_offset`.
  In this suite that is `mfe captions --remap <source_id>`; never hand-compute it.
- **Language pinned.** Auto-detected language can *translate* instead of
  transcribe. Every downstream timestamp is then wrong.
- **Word-level ASR only** where the script supports it. Phrase-level loses the
  sub-second gap data cutting depends on; normalised text loses the restarts.
- **Captions composite last.** One overlay after the caption layer hides it.
- **Burn for social, sidecar for platform.** Deliver `captions.srt` alongside the
  burned file whenever the platform accepts uploads — access beats styling.

## Style, decided once per piece

| Choice | Calm / editorial | High energy / social |
|---|---|---|
| Case | sentence case | CAPS |
| Words per line | 3–5 | 2–3 |
| Weight | regular or medium | bold to black |
| Accent | none, or one word | the active word, every time |
| Background | none | optional 60% box for busy footage |
| Motion | fade 120 ms | 60–90 ms pop on entry, no bounce |

Four rules that hold in both columns:

- **One accent, one use.** If the accent marks the active word, it marks nothing
  else — not keywords, not names, not numbers.
- **Emphasis is rare.** Two or three emphasised words per 30 s. Everything
  emphasised is nothing emphasised.
- **Contrast is non-negotiable.** White on a bright sky fails. Either a shadow, a
  box, or a different position — never "it's probably fine".
- **No emoji unless the brand already uses emoji.** They render as tofu on some
  devices and read as a template on all of them.

## Layout

```
1080×1920
┌──────────────────┐  ← top 12%: platform header, never content
│                  │
│      picture     │
│                  │
│   CAPTION LINE   │  ← lower third: y ≈ 0.68–0.78
│   CAPTION LINE   │     max 2 lines, 3–5 words each
│                  │
├──────────────────┤  ← bottom 23%: caption bar, handle, CTA
└──────────────────┘
```

Keep the caption block inside the middle of the frame horizontally too — the right
13% is the share/like rail. `mfe captions` derives the character budget from the
frame and the margins so lines do not run under it; the gate rejects any cue whose
box leaves the zone.

## Proofreading

Captions are the most-read text you will ever ship, so they get read twice.

- Build a name list **before** rendering: product names, people, tools, jargon.
  Fix them in one pass, not by catching them in review.
- Numbers: prefer digits for data (`40%`, `2.4×`) and words for small counts
  ("three things"). Never mix in one sentence.
- Strip fillers from captions even when they stay in the audio — `um`, false
  starts, and repeated words read as sloppy. The word *timing* stays; only the
  displayed text changes.
- Do not caption `[music]`, `[applause]` or `[laughter]` unless the platform
  requires it for accessibility.

## Accessibility, honestly

- Burned captions are not accessible captions. Ship the `.srt`.
- If a piece is important, say plainly that a human should verify the transcript
  against the audio for names and numbers, because ASR gets exactly those wrong.
- Contrast and size rules are accessibility rules that happen to also look better.


<!-- ===== skills/edit-supervisor/references/sound.md ===== -->
# Sound

You cannot hear the mix. That is the central fact of this file. You have
measurements and a waveform, and you have to be honest about the difference.

## Targets

| Destination | Integrated | True peak | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| TikTok / Reels / Shorts | −14 LUFS | ≤ −1 dBTP | platforms normalise down, never up |
| YouTube long form | −14 LUFS | ≤ −1 dBTP | |
| Podcast / interview | −16 LUFS | ≤ −1 dBTP | mono-ish is fine, dialogue-first |
| Broadcast | −23 LUFS | ≤ −2 dBTP | EBU R128 |
| Any | — | ≤ −1 dBTP | a true peak above 0 clips on encode |

`mfe gate` measures both with `ebur128` and fails outside ±2 LU of target.
Normalise with `loudnorm` in the same pass that composites — not afterwards,
which re-encodes the picture for an audio change.

## The mix, in priority order

```
1  voice          intelligible, consistent, forward
2  music          present, ducked under speech, resolving with the picture
3  sfx            accents on visual events only
4  ambience       only if it establishes a place
```

If you can only get one right, it is the voice. A piece with no music and a clear
voice reads as intentional; a piece with music over a buried voice reads as broken.

## Ducking

Music must drop when the speaker speaks, not sit at one level and fight.

- Static bed under continuous speech: −18 to −22 dB relative to the voice.
- Music-led sections: −10 to −14 dB, with the voice still on top.
- Duck hard on the first syllable after a music-only section; recover over
  250–400 ms, not instantly.
- Sidechain-style ducking with a fast attack (10–30 ms) and slow release
  (300–500 ms) is the difference between "produced" and "two files played at once".

## Making a pop or a sting audible

A sting that is silent in the mix passes every level check, because the loudest
thing in that window is the voice. Measuring the master alone tells you about the
voice, not the effect.

**Measure by differencing.** Render the same window twice — master, and voice-only
cut — and compare. The delta is the sting. Correct for the few dB the render
attenuates the source audio by, measured on sting-free speech windows. A negative
lift is impossible from addition: if you see one, you have not applied that
correction.

Placement beats level:

- A sting lands **1–3 frames before** the visual event, not on it.
- One SFX per visible event. A whoosh on every transition is the single most
  common tell of a machine-made edit.
- Silence is an effect. A 200–400 ms hole before a drop does more than a riser.

## Voice treatment, in order

1. **Clean** — high-pass at 80–100 Hz (removes rumble, keeps body), a gentle
   de-esser if sibilance bites, a de-noise pass *only* if hiss is audible.
2. **Compress** — ratio 3:1, threshold around −18 dB, attack 6 ms, release 110 ms.
   This is for consistency, not loudness.
3. **Limit** — a true-peak limiter at −1 dBTP as the last step, always.
4. **Never** pitch-shift or time-stretch the voice to fit a runtime. Cut words.

Over-processing is worse than no processing: a fully "enhanced" voice sounds
synthetic and immediately reads as AI. If the source is usable, use it.

## What you must say at handoff

One line, every time:

> "Measured −14.2 LUFS, true peak −1.3 dBTP, music ducks 6 dB under speech. I can't
> hear it — check that the music sits under the voice on a phone speaker."

That sentence is the difference between motionframe-edit and wishful thinking.


<!-- ===== skills/edit-supervisor/references/delivery.md ===== -->
# Delivery

A cut file is not a deliverable. The package is.

```
out/
├── <name>-9x16.mp4       the piece, platform-correct
├── <name>-1x1.mp4        variant (optional)
├── <name>-16x9.mp4       variant (optional)
├── captions.srt          uploadable, output-timeline times, proofread
├── thumbnail.jpg         chosen from 3 candidates, checked at small size
├── report.md             every judgement call + every measurement
├── gate-report.json      the audit as data
└── provenance.json       origin of every asset that claims to be real
```

## Encoding

| Field | Vertical social | Landscape |
|---|---|---|
| Codec | H.264 High, yuv420p | H.264 High |
| Bitrate | 10–16 Mbps for 1080×1920 | 16–24 Mbps for 1080p |
| Frame rate | the source's, 30 or 60, constant | constant |
| Audio | AAC 192 kbps, 48 kHz, stereo | same |
| Container | MP4, `+faststart` | MP4, `+faststart` |
| Colour | tagged bt709, no stray HDR | tagged |

Two things that break uploads and never warn you: **variable frame rate** (screen
recordings and phone footage) — force constant; and **odd dimensions** — always
even, yuv420p requires it.

## Variants

Never re-cut for another aspect. Reframe:

- **Same content, different frame.** Re-crop with a subject bias (`fit: "fill"`,
  `framing` per segment) so faces stay centred. Do not letterbox a vertical into
  a landscape — it screams "repost".
- **Re-check safe zones.** The 1:1 and 16:9 safe zones differ; captions that pass
  on 9:16 can sit in the UI on 16:9.
- **Re-audit each variant.** Each is a separate delivery with its own gates.
- **One export per platform, not one export for all.** Bitrate, length and caption
  behaviour differ meaningfully.

## Thumbnails and covers

- Three candidates, generated from real frames at the strongest beats.
- Check at **120 px wide**. If the text is unreadable, it is unreadable.
- One idea per thumbnail: a face, or a claim, or the product. Never all three.
- The hook line is the obvious cover title — reuse it rather than inventing a
  second headline for the same piece.

## report.md

Short, factual, and written for the person publishing, not for you.

```markdown
# <piece> — 52 s, 1080×1920

**Shape**    hook → claim → proof → turn → CTA
**Take choices**  s3 (2nd take of the opening), s7 (last, cleanest read)
**Cut**      11 segments, 40–120 ms padding, cut on silences ≥ 400 ms
**Grade**    neutral_punch, +6 saturation, no hue shift
**Captions** bold-pop, 34 cues, active-word accent, proofread against 9 names
**Sound**    −14.2 LUFS, TP −1.3 dBTP, music −19 dB under voice, 4 SFX
**Audit**    gates G0–G7 pass; 1 warning (end card 9 dB under dialogue, intentional)
**Not checked**  the mix on a phone speaker — needs a human ear
**Open questions**  the third stat needs a real source before publishing
```

## provenance.json

Required whenever any asset could be mistaken for reality.

```json
{ "assets": [
  { "id": "hero-shot",  "origin": "captured",  "source": "real app at 2:14:05",
    "claims_reality": true },
  { "id": "sky-plate",  "origin": "generated", "model": "local", "claims_reality": false },
  { "id": "logo",       "origin": "user",      "claims_reality": true }
]}
```

`origin` ∈ `captured` | `user` | `generated` | `stock-licensed`. A `generated`
asset with `claims_reality: true` fails gate G7 — that is the point.


<!-- ===== skills/motion-director/SKILL.md ===== -->
---
name: motion-director
description: >-
  Design and build motion graphics, animated type, transitions, kinetic captions, logo
  animations, product/launch films, explainer sequences and motion systems. Use for "animate
  this", "add motion graphics", "make a promo/launch film", "make it feel alive", or when
  deciding what should move, in what order, with what easing and for how many frames. Covers
  three render lanes: ffmpeg-native, HTML/GSAP captured in headless Chrome, and React/Remotion.
  All free and local.
license: MIT
---

# Motion director

Motion is not decoration. It is how a piece explains *what changed*, *where the eye
should go*, and *what kind of thing this is*. Motion added for its own sake is the
single fastest way to make work look machine-made.

## Who you are on this job

You are the motion designer, not the animator of last resort. That means:

- You decide **what does not move** first. The motion budget is spent, not filled.
- You build the **hardest beat first**, because it sets the timing of every beat after it.
- You present a **frame-accurate plan** — numbers, not adjectives — before rendering.
- You watch the result at 1× once, end to end, before anyone else sees it.
- If a beat needs a sound you do not have, **the beat changes**. The sound is not faked.

Read `../motionframe-edit/SKILL.md` for the twelve rules. Two matter most here:
**no dead frame**, and **one system per piece**.

## Decide before you animate

All commands below use `$SV` for the engine:

```bash
SV=/absolute/path/to/motionframe-edit/tools/mfe.py   # set once; resolved in skills/motionframe-edit/SKILL.md
```

Answer these five in writing. If you cannot, you are not ready to animate — pick a
different beat to build first.

1. **What changes?** If nothing changes, nothing moves. Motion is a signal.
2. **What does the eye need to see first?** One hero per frame, at most three things.
3. **How long does the viewer's brain need?** Read time is ~200 ms per word plus
   120 ms to acquire a new element. Under that, it is a flash, not a message.
4. **What is the world?** Ground, light, depth, texture. A graphic on nothing is a
   slide.
5. **What is the sound doing?** Words land 0–2 frames before they are heard, not after.

## The five laws of motion

1. **Land decelerates; leave accelerates.** Entries put most of the travel in the
   first 25% of their frames and then ease out with a long tail. Exits ease in
   and leave, or shrink away. Median move ≈ 10 frames at 30 fps. A spring is
   visible at most once per piece — a bounce on everything is a bounce on nothing.
2. **Arrive from oversize, never from zero.** Things crash in from ~3.5×, cursors
   from 2–5×, a thesis word from ~0.39 of the frame height and shrink to place.
   Nothing grows from nothing; that reads as a slide transition.
3. **Shots hand off.** The last frame of beat N is the first frame of beat N+1. A
   carried object, a shared colour, a match cut, a transition that starts in A and
   finishes in B. The logo arrives by cause, never by default.
4. **Cut on motion, never on rest.** Cuts land mid-move; scenes start already
   moving. A piece ends in motion or on a designed stillness — never a default
   fade to black.
5. **Almost nothing fades.** Things arrive by moving, cutting, unmasking or
   focusing. Fades are for a single object or a privacy dissolve, not for a
   scene change and not between every beat.

## Type, colour and layout are not decided here

Motion is one layer over a composition that already has to work as a still. The moment a
frame carries a headline, a lower third, a caption or a grid, the decisions belong to the
design system:

- **Type** — family count, scale ratio, weight pairing, tracking at size: `../design-director/references/system.md`.
- **Colour and contrast** — tokens, not picked-by-eye values; the same file.
- **Whether the frame reads as generic** — `../design-director/references/anti-slop.md`, loaded before the first render, not after.

If a beat needs type bigger than the scale allows, that is a composition problem, not a
licence to break the scale. When the design system and a motion instinct disagree, the ruling
is already written: `references/precedence.md`.

## The decoration test, before you build a single graphic

Every graphic earns its place or it does not get built. Write one line per planned element:

> "After this, the viewer knows ______ that they did not know from the audio."

If the blank restates the voiceover, the element is decoration — cut it now, while it costs
nothing. Two failure shapes to look for, both seen in real renders:

- **The stat card.** A number held on screen that was just spoken. It only earns its place if
  it compares against something (this vs last time, ours vs theirs).
- **The self-citing frame.** `SAMPLE 01`, `TAKE 3`, timecode, HUD corners. That is the look of
  a camera, not of an edit.

The list of what makes a frame read as machine-made is in
`../design-director/references/anti-slop.md` — read it before the beat sheet, not after the
render.

## The beat sheet

Before any code, write a beat sheet. It is the EDL of motion, and it is what makes
a film instead of a pile of animations.

```markdown
| # | beat     | buys            | copy            | moves                        | frames | handoff          |
|---|----------|-----------------|-----------------|------------------------------|--------|------------------|
| 1 | hook     | attention       | "40% wasted"    | number crashes 3.5×→place    | 0–24   | number becomes bar
| 2 | problem  | comprehension   | "…on every call"| bar growth, 12 rows stagger  | 24–76  | bar top → curve
| 3 | proof    | belief          | real UI capture | cursor parks, presses, saves | 76–168 | result → hero card
| 4 | payoff   | the point       | "fixed"         | card shrinks, type arrives   | 168–216| type → lockup
```

Column rules: **buys** is what the viewer gains (attention / comprehension /
belief / desire), and at most 25% of beats are "the point". **frames** is real
arithmetic at the delivery fps. **handoff** cannot be blank — if a beat has no
handoff, it is not a beat, it is a slide.

## Pick a lane

| Lane | Use when | Free toolchain | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — ffmpeg native** | cuts, crops, speed, grade, captions, simple moves (punch, drift, zoom, push), overlays, text cards | ffmpeg only | fastest; limited easing |
| **B — HTML + GSAP** | typography-driven motion, layouts, UI demos, charts, kinetic captions, anything with real DOM | Node + **GSAP** (free) + headless Chrome, frames → ffmpeg | full easing control; needs a browser |
| **C — React / Remotion** | generative/parametric systems, data-driven scenes, many variants from one source, component reuse | Node + **Remotion** (MIT) | most reusable; heaviest setup |

Choose **A** unless the motion needs easing that ffmpeg cannot express — it is
usually enough, and it always ships. Choose **B** for anything type-led. Choose
**C** when you need twenty variants of one scene or the motion is data-driven.

Never mix lanes within one beat. A piece can use A for cuts and B for graphics;
one beat cannot be half in each. Lane details, code patterns and the frame-capture
loop: `references/lanes.md`. Transitions, handoffs and the end: `references/transitions.md`.

## Build the hardest beat first

Not the first beat — the hardest one. Build the hero moment and its hardest
handoff, render stills, and look at them:

```bash
python3 "$SV" sheet --file work/hero.mp4 --out work/hero-sheet.jpg --every 0.2
```

If it does not read at speed, the idea or the staging is wrong, and you find that
out in ten minutes instead of after building the whole piece.

Two structural rules while building:

- **Every frame is a pure function of time.** No state, no accumulation, no
  `setTimeout`. This is what makes a render deterministic, seekable, and
  re-renderable — and it is why Remotion and GSAP timelines both insist on it.
- **Self-test the timeline.** Render frames 0 and N of a move and assert they
  match the plan. A motion that drifts by 2 frames per scene is a mystery at
  minute three.

## Timing vocabulary

Full tables in `references/timing.md`. The short version:

| Intent | Duration @30fps | Easing |
|---|---|---|
| micro-feedback (hover, press) | 4–8 f | ease-out, ≤ 2 px travel |
| UI element enter | 8–14 f | `expo.out` or spring, no overshoot past 4% |
| type line enter | 6–12 f per line, 2–4 f stagger | `power3.out` |
| scene transition | 12–24 f | one grammar, chosen once |
| word on screen | 2–12 f apart | 2–4 f for a fast hook, 8–12 f voice-led |
| hold before payoff | 18–45 f | deliberate, with a reason |
| end hold | 18–42 f | then stop; under 0.6 s ends mid-motion |

Word-level type moves at **speech rhythm**. Whole words, not letter-by-letter —
letter typing belongs only inside the product's own input field, with an authored,
irregular rhythm.

## The gates that apply

Run the standard audit, plus the two motion-specific ones:

```bash
python3 "$SV" gate --file work/draft.mp4 --edl edl.json --out work/gate.json
```

- **G3 picture alive** — no freeze > 0.5 s, no stillness > 3 s. In a motion piece
  this is the "no dead frame" law, measured.
- **G0 duration matches the plan** — a motion piece that overruns its beat sheet is
  usually a beat that got built twice.

By eye, on the contact sheet, ask in this order: is there one hero per frame? does
the eye land where the beat wants it? would any single frame pass as a *slide*? if
yes to the last one, the frame is too static or too page-like.

## Refuse

- An effect with no beat behind it.
- Two effects competing in one frame.
- A transition on every cut.
- A page rendered into a video frame — with margins, a header, a footer, or a
  headline block on the left and media on the right. That is a webpage, not a film.
- Text that exists to fill space rather than to be read.
- Anything you would not watch twice.


<!-- ===== skills/motion-director/references/timing.md ===== -->
# Timing

Numbers here are starting points at **30 fps**, not laws. They are what "feels
right" distilled into something you can type. Deviate with intent, not by accident.

## The three curves you actually need

```
ease-out  (expo/power3.out)   enters, decelerates   ← most arrivals
ease-in   (power2.in)         exits, accelerates   ← leaving shots
ease-in-out (power2.inOut)    A→B repositioning    ← moves that stay on screen
```

Everything else is a variant. Rules:

- **Arrivals** never bounce more than 4% past their target. A UI card that
  overshoots 20% looks broken; a logo that overshoots 4% looks alive.
- **Exits** are ~60% the duration of the matching entrance. Leaving is cheaper
  than arriving, and it keeps the piece moving.
- **Springs** are for physical things the user touched (a drag, a tap, a sheet).
  One spring per piece, at most. A spring on a text line reads as a toy.
- **Linear** is only correct for continuous loops (a marquee, a turntable, a
  progress fill during a real wait).

## Duration by role

| Role | Frames | ms | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| press feedback | 3–5 | 100–170 | must feel instantaneous |
| hover / focus | 4–8 | 130–270 | travel ≤ 2 px |
| tooltip / popover | 8–12 | 270–400 | origin-aware, scale from the trigger |
| modal / sheet | 14–24 | 470–800 | one spring, backdrop fades slower |
| text line in | 6–12 | 200–400 | stagger lines 2–4 f |
| word-level type | 2–12 between words | — | 2–4 fast, 8–12 voice-led |
| image / card entrance | 10–18 | 330–600 | arrive from oversize, never 0 |
| number count-up | 12–30 | 400–1000 | step per frame, land on the spoken value |
| scene change (cut) | 0 | 0 | free, invisible, always available |
| scene change (dissolve/mask) | 12–24 | 400–800 | only on a change of world |
| hold before payoff | 18–45 | 600–1500 | needs a stated reason |
| end hold | 18–42 | 600–1400 | under 0.6 s ends mid-motion |

## Stagger and choreography

Stagger is how a group reads as one thing instead of a list:

- **Rows/lines:** 2–4 frames apart, total under 12 frames. More than that and the
  eye follows the stagger instead of the content.
- **Grids/cards:** 1–2 frames per item, diagonal order, total under 20 frames.
- **Subordination:** the hero moves 100%, its supports 40%, the ground 0%. If
  everything moves, nothing leads.
- **Overlap:** start the next element at 70–80% of the previous one's duration.
  Simultaneous is mechanical; strictly sequential is slow.
- **What stays still** is a choreography decision. Choose at least one thing that
  does not move, so the movement has a reference.

## Easing tables by feel

Because "make it snappier" is a direction, not a number:

| Direction | Change |
|---|---|
| snappier / punchier | duration ×0.7, keep the curve, add 0–2 f of anticipation |
| slower / more premium | duration ×1.4, switch to expo.out, reduce travel |
| more playful | one small overshoot (≤4%), stagger ×1.5 |
| more expensive | less travel, longer tails, fewer simultaneous moves |
| less busy | delete a move entirely before shortening it |

**Deleting a move is almost always the right answer to "too busy".**

## The read-time budget

The viewer needs time to *acquire* and time to *read*:

```
acquire  ≈ 120 ms   (a new element appearing somewhere new)
read     ≈ 200 ms/word  (short words are cheaper, numbers are slower)
```

So a 4-word claim needs ~0.9 s on screen after it has settled, and a number needs
~0.5 s. Anything under budget is a flash; anything over 3× budget is a pause that
reads as an error. This is why "no more than 3–4 s without a change" works in
short form: the budget runs out before the patience does.

## Frame-exactness checks

Three checks catch nearly all motion bugs:

1. **First frame of a move** is the intended start pose — not 20% in.
   For ffmpeg overlays that means `setpts=PTS-STARTPTS+T/TB` shifting the overlay
   so its frame 0 lands on the window start.
2. **Last frame** is the settled pose, fully resolved, no half-eased remainder.
3. **Determinism**: render the same frame twice; it must be identical. If it is
   not, some state leaked into the animation.


<!-- ===== skills/motion-director/references/transitions.md ===== -->
# Transitions and handoffs

The default is the **hard cut**. It is free, invisible, and works in every piece
ever made. Everything below is a deliberate exception.

## The hierarchy

```
1  hard cut                  default, no cost
2  cut on motion             invisible, reads as one continuous move
3  match cut                 same shape/colour/motion across a shot change
4  carried object            something travels from beat N into beat N+1
5  mask / wipe               a designed reveal, on a change of idea
6  dissolve                  a change of world or time, never a change of shot
7  fade to black             only if the brand earned it, and almost never
```

Every step down costs attention. Spending 1–2 per piece is usually right.

## Cut on motion

The cheapest way to make cutting feel expensive: land the cut **mid-move**. A hand
in motion becomes a different hand in motion; a pan becomes a different pan. The
eye reads continuity where there is none.

Practical rules:

- Find the frame where motion is fastest, not where it settles.
- Cut within 2–3 frames of the motion peak.
- Match the *direction* of movement across the cut, not the subject.
- Never cut into a static frame and out of a static frame — that is two fades with
  extra steps.

## Handoffs

A handoff is what makes a sequence a film. Three reliable forms:

| Form | Mechanic | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| carried object | one element travels through every seam (a card, a cursor, a colour) | the eye tracks it, so the cut is free |
| shape match | a circle in A becomes the counter of a letter in B | the brain sees one continuous form |
| cause and effect | A sets something in motion, B is the consequence, with 1–2 f of overlap | logic covers the seam |

Every beat in the sheet must name its handoff. If a beat has none, it is a slide.

## Masks and wipes

A mask that reveals the next shot in a *meaningful direction* reads as designed;
a random wipe reads as a plugin.

- Reveal along the reading direction (left→right in LTR scripts).
- The mask shape should echo something in the content (a doorway, a bar chart's
  column, a progress edge).
- Keep it ≤ 24 frames. Past that, it is a transition the audience watches instead
  of the content.
- End the mask on a *live* frame of the next shot, never on a still.

## Audio-led transitions

The most underused tool. A change of shot on a sound event costs nothing visually
and lands harder than any wipe:

- Cut picture 1–3 frames before the transient.
- Keep the outgoing audio 2–4 frames into the incoming picture (an L-cut): the ear
  accepts what the eye just left.
- A hole in the music before a drop does more than a riser over it.

## The end

The last two seconds are part of the design.

- End in motion, or on a designed stillness of 0.6–1.4 s. Under 0.6 s the piece
  ends mid-motion; over 1.4 s it ends in a hold that reads as a stalled player.
- The end card / logo arrives by cause — it is what the motion built to, not a
  separate slide appended at the end.
- The final shot should be at most ~25% of the runtime. A long tail is where
  retention dies.
- Never fade to black as a default ending. It says "the file ran out".


<!-- ===== skills/motion-director/references/lanes.md ===== -->
# The three lanes

One motion spec, three ways to execute it. Choosing well is most of the schedule.

## Lane A — ffmpeg native

**Best for:** cuts, crops, punch-ins, drifts, speed ramps, grades, captions,
text cards, logo overlays, simple overlays, anything under ~30 s of motion.

```bash
# punch-in on an emphasis word, easing baked into keyframes is not available —
# so use a short, small move; a 106% push over 8 frames reads as intentional
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "scale=1088:1936,crop=1080:1920:x='(iw-ow)/2':y='(ih-oh)/2'" out.mp4

# slow drift over a held shot (the "no dead frame" fix)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "zoompan=z='min(1.00+0.0008*on,1.10)':d=1:s=1080x1920:fps=30" out.mp4

# overlay a rendered animation, frame 0 at t=2.0  ← the classic silent failure
ffmpeg -i base.mp4 -i anim.mov -filter_complex \
 "[1:v]trim=duration=3,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS+2.0/TB,format=rgba[ov];[0:v][ov]overlay=enable='between(t,2.0,5.0)'" out.mp4
```

Grudging but correct. Easing is limited to what filters express; `zoompan`,
`xfade`, `curves` and `sendcmd` cover more than people expect. If you need real
easing curves, stop and use lane B.

## Lane B — HTML + GSAP + headless Chrome

**Best for:** type-led motion, layouts, UI demos, charts, kinetic captions,
anything that would be a webpage if it stood still.

The loop is: a deterministic HTML page where **time is an input**, a headless
browser that can render frame N on demand, and ffmpeg to assemble.

```html
<!-- film.html — every frame is a pure function of t -->
<script src="gsap.min.js"></script>
<script>
const M = { beat: 2.0, title: 3.4, out: 6.0 };      // the motion spec, one place
function seek(t) {
  const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
  tl.from(".num",   { scale: 3.5, opacity: 0, duration: 0.4, ease: "expo.out" }, 0)
    .from(".claim", { y: 40, opacity: 0, duration: 0.5, ease: "power3.out" }, 0.35)
    .to(".card",    { scale: 0.94, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.in" }, M.out - 0.3);
  tl.seek(t);                                       // exact, seekable, repeatable
  return tl;
}
window.__render = (t) => { seek(t); return true; };
</script>
```

Capture frames with a headless browser you already have, then encode:

```bash
# determinism first: the same t must produce the same pixels, twice in a row
node -e "/* puppeteer/playwright: page.evaluate(t => window.__render(t), 1.2) → screenshot */"
ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i frames/%05d.png -c:v libx264 -crf 16 -pix_fmt yuv420p out.mp4
```

Rules that make lane B reliable:

- **Never** use CSS transitions or `requestAnimationFrame` for scene motion. They
  are wall-clock; you need virtual time.
- **Disable font loading races** — embed fonts as base64, or wait for
  `document.fonts.ready` before the first frame.
- **Fixed viewport, fixed device scale factor**, `--force-device-scale-factor=1`.
  A 2× capture that gets resampled later looks soft at exactly the moment it
  matters.
- **Deterministic textures**: no `Math.random()` without a seed, no video elements,
  no live data.
- Two frames of overlap on every seek is cheap insurance against a rounding error.

## Lane C — React / Remotion

**Best for:** parametric systems, data-driven scenes, many variants from one
source, a component library of moves.

```tsx
// one composition, N variants — this is what lane C is actually for
export const Scene: React.FC<{ variant: Variant }> = ({ variant }) => {
  const frame = useCurrentFrame();
  const { fps } = useVideoConfig();
  const enter = interpolate(frame, [0, 0.5 * fps], [3.5, 1],
                            { easing: Easing.out(Easing.expo), extrapolateRight: "clamp" });
  return <div style={{ transform: `scale(${enter})` }}>{variant.copy}</div>;
};
```

Remotion is MIT-licensed and free for individuals and small teams; check its
current licence terms before commercial use, and note that other tools in this
space are not free — prefer lane B when in doubt, it has no licence question at
all.

Rules: `useCurrentFrame()` only, no `useState` for visual values, no timers, no
network. Every parameter that changes between variants belongs in props, not in
the component.

## Choosing, in one table

| Need | Lane |
|---|---|
| cut, crop, caption, grade | A |
| 2–10 s of type motion | B |
| a UI demo where real DOM helps | B |
| 20 variants of one animated card | C |
| data-driven scene at scale | C |
| no Node available | A |
| a client who needs the source project | B |

## The frame handoff between lanes

Lane B and C render to video, then lane A composites them. Two rules:

1. **Match the delivery fps and frame size exactly** at render time. Resampling a
   motion graphic is how it gets soft edges at the worst moment.
