2. **Render motion with an alpha channel** if it composites over footage —
   `-c:v qtrle` (lossless RGBA) or ProRes 4444, never a codec that drops alpha.
    For long graphics, render `png` sequences instead; disk is cheaper than a
    re-render.


<!-- ===== skills/design-director/SKILL.md ===== -->
---
name: design-director
description: >-
  Art direction for pages, products, UIs, posters, decks, thumbnails and brand systems — and the
  critique of work that looks "AI-made", templated, generic or over-designed. Use when designing
  or reviewing anything visual that is not primarily footage or motion: landing pages, app
  screens, brand identity, type and colour systems, layout, imagery and asset policy. Enforces
  the anti-slop rules and resolves conflicting taste advice with one precedence ladder.
license: MIT
---

# Design director

The failure this skill exists to prevent is not ugliness. It is **genericity**: the
page, deck or poster that could belong to any company, made of the same rounded
cards, the same purple gradient, the same three-feature grid, and the same
confident sentence that says nothing.

The bar, in words: a good company would ship this, and a stranger could tell who it
is for.

Read `../motionframe-edit/SKILL.md` for the twelve rules. Rule 8 (the precedence ladder)
and law 9 (one system) do most of the work here.

## Step 0 — name the kind of thing it is

Most design failures are a mismatch between kind and treatment: a shader effect on
a bakery, photographs on a developer tool. Decide the kind first, in writing, and
let it drive every later choice.

| Brief | Kind | The page leads with |
|---|---|---|
| app, SaaS, AI, dev tool, fintech | **software** | its own real UI, at true size, doing the actual work |
| game, game studio | **gaming** | the game's world, full-bleed key art |
| hardware, device, gadget | **tech-product** | the object, whole, big, in a real setting |
| any other physical product | **product** | the product photographed or rendered, big |
| clinic, law firm, agency, studio | **service** | the people and the work |
| cafe, bar, bakery, guesthouse, shop | **place** | 12–20 real photographs and the address |

Then apply the consequences, which are strict:

- **Place** gets photographs, flat colour, type, real icons and a quiet hover layer.
  **No** shader effects, no gradient grounds, no "moments", no scenes.
- **Software/gaming/tech** may spend the one-effect budget — a shader ground, one
  WebGL object, one big scene — because the subject is technical and the audience
  expects it.
- **A physical product with no photographs** gets a render (or a diagram), never a
  stock mood shot and never a drawn SVG pretending to be the product.

## Step 1 — the one thing

Write, in four lines, before any layout:

```
Problem    what is broken or missing for this audience
Audience   who specifically, and what they already believe
Goal       the one action this page or piece exists to cause
Emotion    the one feeling that makes the action easy

Then: the ONE real thing this is about — a feature, a moment, a photo, a claim.
```

If the one thing is vague ("we help teams collaborate better"), the design will be
vague no matter how good the typography is. Fix the sentence, then design.

## Step 2 — material, honestly

Inventory what actually exists: logo (official file), screens, photographs,
prices, address, hours, real numbers, real quotes. Then place each on the asset
ladder and never skip down more than one rung:

```
real capture / real photograph
  → official asset from the brand
    → render or diagram of the real thing
      → typographic treatment
        → generated image (never implying reality)
```

Two rules with no exceptions:

- **Never invent facts.** No invented metrics, logos, testimonials, addresses or
  phone numbers. If a number is needed and missing, write less, not fiction.
- **Never fabricate proof.** A generated image may be a mood, a texture, an
  impossible object. It may never be a screenshot, a dashboard, a person's words,
  or a product that does not exist. Declare it in `provenance.json`.

## Step 3 — the system, before the page

```
grid        one column count, one gutter, one max width
type        one family (two at most), one scale, ≤ 4 sizes in use
colour      neutrals + exactly one accent with exactly one meaning
space       one spacing step (4 or 8 px) — no 13px, no 27px
radius      one value, or two (control, container)
elevation   at most two levels, and prefer a border to a shadow
icon        one icon set, real product icons where a real product is named
```

Write it as tokens and use only tokens. Details and the exact scales:
`references/system.md`.

The test: change one token, and the whole piece should update coherently. If a
value is hardcoded anywhere, the system is decorative.

## Step 4 — layout that behaves

- **One idea per screen.** A hero alone on the first screen; each section one or
  two screens tall at 1440×900; no second section heading peeking in.
- **Equal content edges** left and right. Asymmetry must be a decision with a
  reason, not a default that drifted.
- **One focal point per frame** — one hero, at most three elements competing.
- **Empty space must do a job.** If it is empty because nothing filled it, that is
  a hole, not whitespace.
- **Every visual renders.** No placeholder boxes, no empty image frames, at any of
  1440 / 1024 / 768 / 390 px.
- **The mobile view is the design**, not a squeezed desktop.

## Step 5 — copy is design

Half of "this looks AI-made" is the words. The rules:

- The headline names the category and the buyer, or the place. Not a feeling.
- One hard fact on the first screen — a number, a name, a price, a location.
- A noun in every heading. "Built for the way you work" is a mood; "Offline-first
  notes for field crews" is a page.
- Buttons are a verb and an object: "Book a room", "Start free trial",
  "Get directions". Never "Learn more" as the primary action.
- 60–80 words per screen for software; fewer for a place, where photographs speak.
- No sentence that could appear on a competitor's page unchanged. That test kills
  most copy, and it should.

## Step 6 — the polish layer

This is where work stops feeling generated. All of it is cheap, none of it is
optional:

- A linked card lifts 1–2 px on hover; a photograph zooms 1.02–1.03 inside its frame.
- Buttons step on hover, compress 1 px on press. Focus rings are visible and never
  removed.
- Underlines draw on hover, from the same direction as reading.
- Transitions are 130–270 ms and never animate layout properties.
- Every state exists: empty, loading, error, one item, a thousand items,
  unbroken text (a 40-character email), missing fields, offline.
- The tab title, favicon, social card and 404 exist and match.

Motion specifics for interfaces: `../ui-motion/SKILL.md`. It is the authority on
timing; this skill is the authority on everything around it.

## Step 7 — look, then fix

1. Screenshot at 1440, 1024, 768, 390. Look at all four.
2. Squint at the thumbnail. Can you tell what is being sold? If not, the hierarchy
   is wrong — not the type size.
3. Cover the headline. Does the picture still say something? If not, the image is
   decoration.
4. Swap the logo for a competitor's. If the page still works, the design is generic.
   That is the test, and it is brutal by design.
5. Fix in order: untrue or broken → the idea → hierarchy → spacing → type → colour
   → surface → motion.

The anti-slop checklist, with the exact tells and their fixes:
`references/anti-slop.md`. Read it before shipping, not before starting.

## Refuse

- Three identical feature cards, or a three-column grid with icons.
- A gradient as a button, a border, or text.
- Two accents, or an accent with no meaning.
- Stock photography of people pointing at laptops.
- An emoji as an icon; a drawn icon for a product that has a real one.
- Centred body text; justified text; grey-on-grey.
- A carousel, a timed tab switcher, a scroll-jacked section.
- Placeholder copy, lorem ipsum, or "Coming soon" where the real thing belongs.
- A dark hero and a gradient glow because the reference had one.

## Deliver

For a page: the files, plus a one-screen `DESIGN.md` recording the kind, the one
thing, the tokens, the asset provenance, and what you could not verify.

For a critique: verdict, ranked problems with evidence (a screenshot region or a
number), and the five fixes to do first. Never a compliment sandwich — say what
works once, then spend the rest on what does not, with fixes.


<!-- ===== skills/design-director/references/anti-slop.md ===== -->
# Anti-slop

Slop is not one mistake. It is a set of tells that individually look fine and
together say "nobody was here". This is the checklist, with the fix for each.

## The tells, in order of how often they appear

| # | Tell | Why it reads as machine-made | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Three identical feature cards with icons | the layout is the default of every template ever made | make one thing the hero; give the other two asymmetric weight, or use a real screenshot instead of an icon |
| 2 | Purple/violet gradient on a dark hero | the house style of 2023–24 AI startups | a real product image, or flat ink on paper colour |
| 3 | A rounded card in a rounded panel on a grey ground | three levels of containment saying nothing | flatten: one container, one border, no nesting |
| 4 | Emoji as an icon (🚀 ⚡ ✨) | renders inconsistently, reads as a template | a real icon set, or nothing |
| 5 | "Built for the way you work" / "The future of X" | a headline with no noun | name the category and the buyer |
| 6 | Centred everything, equal spacing everywhere | no hierarchy, so the eye has nowhere to land | one left-aligned column, deliberate asymmetry in scale |
| 7 | Glassmorphism / blur panels | costs performance, signals "demo" | solid surface, real contrast |
| 8 | Icons drawn for products that have real ones | looks like the wrong company | official asset from the brand, or write the name |
| 9 | Two accents, or an accent used for links and buttons and highlights | nothing means anything | one accent, one meaning |
| 10 | Stock photos of people at laptops, handshakes, city skylines | the reader knows they are not your product | real photographs, or no photographs |
| 11 | Constant motion on scroll (parallax on everything) | motion without state change | decorative motion only where there is an effect budget |
| 12 | Placeholder text anywhere in a shipped artifact | obviously unfinished | write the real sentence, or remove the element |
| 13 | A "moment" on a local business page (a shader, a WebGL object) | the wrong register: a cafe is not a product launch | photographs, flat colour, type |
| 14 | Borders of 1px on everything, shadows on everything | no surface hierarchy | pick one method for elevation and stick to it |
| 15 | Text over a busy photo with no scrim | unreadable, immediately | a gradient scrim, a solid panel, or a different crop |
| 16 | The same section structure twice | reads as an unfinished template | deal each section a different composition |
| 17 | Numbers with no source ("10x faster") | an invented metric is the worst kind of slop | a real number, with a real source, or none |
| 18 | Letter-by-letter typing effect on a headline | a 2010s tell | whole words, or nothing |

## The three tests

Run all three. They are fast and they do not lie.

**1. The competitor swap.** Replace the logo and the product name with a
competitor's. If the page still works, it was never *for* anyone. Fix: specificity
in copy, imagery and the one thing.

**2. The cover test.** Cover the headline with your hand. Does the picture alone
say what this is? If not, the image is decoration and the page is a template with a
paragraph.

**3. The thumbnail test.** Shrink to 120 px wide. Can you still tell what is being
sold? If not, the hierarchy is broken — often because the hero is a decorative
gradient and the actual product is a small card below the fold.

## Register: the most common real mistake

The same "expensive" treatment reads as *good* on one kind of business and
*absurd* on another. Getting the register wrong is worse than being plain.

| Kind | What works | What is wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Software / AI / dev tool | its own UI at true size, dense real detail, one shader ground | a stock photo of a "team" |
| Hardware | the object, whole, in a real place, with real scale | a floating render on a gradient |
| Product (food, clothes, furniture) | real photographs, honest colour, the thing in use | a drawn SVG of the product |
| Service (clinic, law, agency) | the people, the work, the address, credentials | a glowing dashboard mockup |
| Place (cafe, bakery, guesthouse) | 12–20 real photographs, the address set large, hours, one action | any effect; any WebGL; any "moment" |

## What "expensive" actually means

Not effects. Rather:

- **Less, done precisely.** One font. Four sizes. One accent. Every value from a token.
- **Real material.** A real product, a real place, a real person, a real number.
- **Tight craft at small sizes.** Optical alignment, consistent optical margin,
  no orphan words, no 1px misalignments, correct apostrophes.
- **Confidence through restraint.** A large headline with nothing competing
  beside it, and a lot of honest space.
- **One deviation.** A single unexpected move — a huge number, an oddly cropped
  photograph, one bold colour — against an otherwise quiet system. That is what
  people remember, and it only works if it is the only one.

## Two that come back from source material, because they are what video slop looks like

Motion work fails differently from page work, and the sources said so before we did. Both of
these were in the material and neither survived the first merge — which is why a render can
now pass every mechanical gate and still read as machine-made.

| # | Pattern | Why it reads as slop | Instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | **Production metadata as decoration** — `SAMPLE 01`, `TAKE 3`, `FILM 01`, `01 / 04`, version numbers, timecode, HUD corners | It is the look of a design tool, not of a finished piece. The viewer learns nothing and the frame gets busier | Nothing. The frame does not need to cite itself |
| 19 | **A stat card that restates what was just said** — big number over a small label ("Pause 1.57 s") | A number on screen only earns its place if it compares, ranks, or proves something the audio does not already carry. Otherwise it is a wall of self-important decoration | Show the comparison, or cut the card. One number that lands beats five that decorate |

## Pre-ship checklist

- [ ] Could this be a competitor's page with the logo swapped? → fix specificity
- [ ] Renders at 1440 / 1024 / 768 / 390 with no empty frames
- [ ] One accent, one meaning; one type scale; one spacing step
- [ ] Every heading has a noun; every button is verb + object
- [ ] No invented number, quote, logo, address, or screenshot
- [ ] Every external asset has a declared origin
- [ ] All states exist: empty, loading, error, one item, 1000 items, long text
- [ ] Focus rings visible; contrast ≥ 4.5:1 for body text
- [ ] Reduced-motion honoured: no essential information in motion only
- [ ] The one deviation is genuinely only one


<!-- ===== skills/design-director/references/system.md ===== -->
# The system

A design system is not a component library. It is the small set of decisions that
make every later decision cheaper and more consistent.

## Type

**One family.** Two only if one is a display cut of the other. Free, high quality,
open-licensed: Inter, Source Sans 3, IBM Plex, Instrument Sans, Fraunces,
Newsreader, JetBrains Mono.

```
scale (1.25 ratio, fluid between 390 and 1440)
  display   clamp(2.5rem, 6vw, 5rem)     leading 0.95–1.05, tracking −0.02em
  h1        clamp(2rem, 4vw, 3rem)       leading 1.05,      tracking −0.015em
  h2        clamp(1.5rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)   leading 1.15,      tracking −0.01em
  body      1rem–1.0625rem               leading 1.55,      tracking 0
  small     0.875rem                     leading 1.45
  mono      0.875rem                     for code, data, IDs
```

Five rules that do 80% of the work:

1. **Body text never below 16 px**, never above ~72 characters per line.
2. **Left-aligned.** Centred body copy and justified text are tells.
3. **Optical size relationships:** the display is 3–5× the body, not 1.6×. Weak
   contrast in scale is what "corporate" means.
4. **Never two weights in one line**, and never bold for more than ~8 words.
5. **Correct punctuation**: curly apostrophes, en dashes for ranges, no double
   spaces, no ALL CAPS for a long heading (tracked caps only for ≤ 3 words).

## Colour

```
ink-900  #0E0E10   text, primary
ink-600  #52525B   secondary text
ink-300  #D4D4D8   borders, dividers
paper    #FAFAF9   ground
surface  #FFFFFF   cards when a card is genuinely needed
accent   #     1  THE accent — one meaning, stated in DESIGN.md
semantic ok/warn/error — not accents, never decorative
```

- **One accent, one meaning.** "This is actionable", or "this is AI", or "this is
  on". Pick one. Not all three.
- **Contrast:** body ≥ 4.5:1, large text ≥ 3:1, UI borders ≥ 3:1 against their
  own background. Grey-on-grey is a defect, not a style.
- **Dark mode is a second design**, not an inversion. Surfaces are lighter than
  the ground, elevation comes from lightness not shadow, and the accent usually
  needs desaturating.
- **Gradients** are a ground, never a control. One per piece. Never on a place page.
- **Colour is never the only signal.** State must have a shape, an icon or a label
  too.

## Space

One step. 4 px, or 8 px. Everything is a multiple.

```
2 4 8 12 16 24 32 48 64 96 128 192
```

Section padding: 96–192 px desktop, 48–96 mobile. Component padding: 8–24.
Gap between related items: 8–12. Between groups: 32–48. Between sections: 96+.

**Whitespace is hierarchy.** If two elements are 20 px apart, they read as related.
If they are 96 px apart, they read as separate ideas. Nothing should be 37 px apart.

## Grid and measure

- 12-column grid, one max width (1080–1280 px for marketing, 1440 for apps),
  one gutter (24–32 px).
- Equal left and right content edges. Full-bleed elements break the grid on
  purpose and only once or twice.
- Stack to one column below 768 px, and check that the *order* still makes sense —
  mobile is not a squeezed desktop.

## Surfaces, radii, elevation

- Pick one containment method: a border, or a background change, or a shadow.
  Mixing all three is the "rounded card in a rounded panel" tell.
- One radius for controls, one for containers (or a single value for both).
  Pills for tags and avatars only.
- Two elevation levels maximum. Prefer a 1 px border over a shadow for anything
  that is not actually floating.
- Never nest more than one rounded container.

## Icons and imagery

- **One icon set**, one stroke width, one corner treatment. Real product logos only
  from official files — never redrawn, never generated.
- Photographs: real ones, cropped decisively, at least two per screen on a product
  page, and a different picture in every section.
- Every image has a `width`, `height` and a meaningful `alt`. Decorative images use
  `alt=""`.
- Aspect ratios from a small set (1:1, 4:5, 3:2, 16:9). Mixed ratios in one row is
  the fastest way to look unfinished.

## Tokens or nothing

```css
:root {
  --ink: #0E0E10; --ink-2: #52525B; --line: #D4D4D8;
  --paper: #FAFAF9; --surface: #FFFFFF;
  --accent: #1F6FEB;            /* one meaning: "actionable" */
  --step: 8px;
  --r-control: 8px; --r-container: 16px;
  --f-display: clamp(2.5rem, 6vw, 5rem);
  --t-fast: 130ms; --t-base: 200ms; --t-slow: 270ms;
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1);
}
```

If a raw hex, a raw px and a raw ms appear in a component, the system has failed
and the piece will drift. Grep for them before you ship.


<!-- ===== skills/ui-motion/SKILL.md ===== -->
---
name: ui-motion
description: >-
  Interface animation and interaction craft — deciding whether something should animate at all,
  then how: timing, springs, choreography, gestures, reduced motion and frame-budget performance.
  Use when building or reviewing app/website motion, popovers, sheets, drag interactions, page
  transitions, hover and press feedback, or when an interface feels "floaty", "cheap", "slow" or
  "janky". Apple-grade fluidity on a web frame budget.
license: MIT
---

# UI motion

An interface that moves well feels physical and inevitable. One that moves badly
feels like a slideshow with opinions. The difference is almost never the library.

## Should it animate at all?

Ask in this order. The first "no" means do not animate it.

1. **Did something change that the user did not do?** → animate it in (they need to
   know it appeared, and where from).
2. **Did the user just do it?** → animate only if the change is instant-but-continuous
   (a drag, a knob, a scroll). Continuity, not decoration.
3. **Is it on a high-frequency surface?** (a key repeat, a table sort, a keystroke,
   a hover trail) → **no.** Frequency and motion are inversely proportional: the
   more often it happens, the less it should move.
4. **Does it communicate a relationship?** (this panel came from that button; this
   row moved to that list) → yes, and the motion must show the relationship.
5. **Is it purely decorative?** → no, unless it is the one moment the piece is
   allowed and it costs no frames.

## The timing table

| Interaction | Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| press / tap feedback | 100–170 ms | must feel instantaneous; transform only |
| hover | 130–270 ms | travel ≤ 2 px; never animate box-shadow |
| tooltip | 270–400 ms | origin-aware, no delay on show if it followed a click |
| popover / dropdown | 270–400 ms | scale from the trigger corner, 0.96 → 1 |
| sheet / modal | 470–800 ms | one spring; backdrop fades 1.4× slower than the panel |
| page / route | 200–400 ms | content in, chrome stays put |
| list reorder | 200–350 ms | items move along the shortest path |
| expand / collapse | 250–400 ms | animate `transform` + `scaleY`, never `height` |

Above 800 ms is a deliberate, watched moment. Below 100 ms nothing is perceived
as motion — either use no transition, or make it 130 ms and feel intentional.

## The four rules that prevent "floaty"

1. **One spring, at most, per view.** Springs are for physical things the user
   manipulated. A spring on a text label reads as a toy.
2. **Motion is proportional to distance.** A 4 px move is not 400 ms. Above 40 px of
   travel, add no more than 100 ms per additional 100 px.
3. **Everything that enters exits the same way.** Same curve, same duration,
   reversed. Consistency is what reads as craft.
4. **The end pose is exact.** No half-eased remainder, no 0.998 scale. Set the
   final state explicitly.

## Origin and relationship

The most legible motion in an interface is *where things came from*:

- A popover scales from the corner nearest its trigger, not from its centre.
- A detail view expands from the card that was tapped (a shared-element
  transition), not by sliding in from the right edge.
- A moved row animates along the path it actually took.
- A deleted item shrinks toward the trash, or toward where it went — not straight
  down and out.

If you cannot state the relationship, the animation is decoration. Delete it.

## What to animate (and what never to)

**Animate:** `transform` (translate, scale, rotate), `opacity`, `filter` (sparingly —
blur is expensive), `clip-path` (for reveals).

**Never animate:** `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding`, `border-width`,
`box-shadow`, `background-position`, or anything that forces layout or paint on
every frame. These are the reason interfaces feel janky on real hardware.

Never `transition: all`. It is the same thing as "animate whatever happens", which
is what "cheap" means.

## Gestures

- **Track the finger 1:1** while dragging. Any easing during the drag feels broken.
- **On release, decide in one frame:** commit if past threshold or fast enough
  (velocity matters more than distance), else spring back.
- **Interruptible.** A second gesture during an animation takes over from the
  current visual position, never from the animation's start.
- **Rubber-band past the boundary** by ~12% of the travel, then resist.
- **Haptic/visual acknowledgement on the frame the gesture is recognised**, not
  when the animation completes.

## Reduced motion is not optional

Respect `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`:

- Remove all decorative motion, parallax, and auto-playing movement.
- Keep state changes, but make them instant, or use a 100 ms opacity change.
- **No information may be conveyed by motion alone.** If the user cannot see the
  animation, they must still understand the outcome.
- Never hide content behind an intersection-observer reveal that also fails for
  reduced motion — the classic bug where the page looks empty.

## The frame budget

At 60 fps you have 16.7 ms per frame. Real hardware (a mid-range Android, a
thermal-throttled laptop) has less. So:

- Composite-only properties keep the work off the main thread.
- Blur, large shadows, and 3+ simultaneous transforms will drop frames.
- Animate at most 2–3 elements simultaneously; stagger the rest.
- Test with 6× CPU throttling. If it holds, it ships.

Details, spring maths and a performance audit procedure: `references/craft.md`.

## Reviewing motion (yours or someone else's)

Do not say "feels off". Say which of these it is:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| floaty | duration too long, or easing too soft | ×0.7 duration, `expo.out` |
| cheap | spring on everything, or `transition: all` | one spring max, explicit properties |
| janky | animating layout/paint properties | transform/opacity only |
| confusing | origin or relationship unstated | animate from the trigger |
| slow | over 400 ms on a frequent interaction | halve it |
| distracting | high-frequency surface, or no state change | remove it |
| broken | end pose inexact, or not interruptible | set final state, take over on gesture |
| inaccessible | motion is the only signal | add a static state change |

Default to flagging. Approval must be earned, not inferred.


<!-- ===== skills/ui-motion/references/craft.md ===== -->
# Craft notes: springs, choreography, performance

## Springs in practice

A spring has three useful parameters and no more: **stiffness**, **damping**, **mass**.
Think in behaviour, not numbers:

| Feel | stiffness / damping / mass | Use |
|---|---|---|
| precise, near-instant | 400 / 30 / 1 | controls, toggles |
| natural, slight settle | 260 / 24 / 1 | sheets, modals, cards |
| lazy, heavy | 170 / 20 / 1 | large surfaces, drawers |
| playful (use once, never twice) | 300 / 16 / 1 | one hero moment |

Rules:

- **Overshoot ≤ 4%** for anything with text in it. Text that bounces past its
  resting position is unreadable for 100 ms, and 100 ms is a long time.
- **Settling time matters more than curve shape.** If it takes more than ~600 ms to
  be visually at rest, it is too slow, whatever it looks like frame by frame.
- **Springs do not take a duration.** If your API wants both a spring and a
  duration, you are holding two contradictory models; pick one.
- Never run a spring on a value a user is currently dragging.

## Choreography

A group of elements moving together needs a lead, a follow, and something still.

```
lead      the hero: 100% of the travel, longest tail
follow    the supports: 40% travel, stagger 2–4 f
still     the ground: 0
```

- **Overlap, do not queue.** Start element 2 at 70–80% of element 1's duration.
  Fully sequential feels like a loading sequence; fully simultaneous has no lead.
- **Stagger is a rhythm, not a constant.** 2–4 frames per item, capping the total
  under ~12 frames; beyond that the eye follows the stagger instead of the content.
- **Direction follows reading order** (left→right, top→bottom) unless the content
  has its own flow — then follow the content.
- **Interrupt gracefully.** If the user acts mid-choreography, snap everything to
  its end state instantly rather than finishing the show.

## Gesture physics

```
commit if:  distance > 35% of the travel  OR  velocity > 0.5 px/ms in that direction
otherwise:  spring back with the sheet's own spring

drag:       1:1, no easing, no smoothing
boundary:   rubber-band at ~12% of travel, then asymptote
release:    decide in one frame, animate from current position
cancel:     reverse from current position (never from 0)
```

The single most common gesture bug: releasing and animating back to the *start*
instead of continuing from where the finger left it. That one bug makes an
interface feel broken even when the rest is perfect.

## Performance audit

1. **Record a performance profile** while doing the interaction, on 6× CPU
   throttling. Not on your machine at 1×.
2. Look for **long frames** (> 16.7 ms) and read what caused them: layout, paint,
   or composite. Composite-only means the animation itself is fine.
3. Check for **layout thrash**: reading `getBoundingClientRect()` inside a scroll or
   drag handler, then writing styles. Batch reads, then writes, or use
   `ResizeObserver`.
4. Check for **layer explosion**: too many `will-change` declarations, or
   `transform: translateZ(0)` sprinkled everywhere. Each layer costs memory; on a
   low-end device this is where the jank lives.
5. Check **image decoding** — a large image first rendered during an animation is an
   instant dropped frame. Decode before you animate (`img.decode()`).
6. Re-test with **reduced motion on** and with the network throttled.

## Accessibility, concretely

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}
```

That rule handles the crude case. It is not enough on its own, because:

- Content revealed by scroll must be visible without the observer firing
  (a `no-js`/reduced-motion fallback that sets `opacity: 1`).
- A state change signalled only by motion (a shake for "wrong") must also have a
  text or colour change.
- Focus movement must never depend on an animation completing. Move focus
  immediately; animate the visuals around it.
- Auto-playing motion over 5 s needs a pause control.

## The invisible details that read as quality

Cheap to add, immediately felt:

- The press state starts on `pointerdown`, not on `click`.
- Hover out is faster than hover in (by ~30%).
- A sheet's backdrop and its content do not move together; the backdrop lags.
- Focus rings never disappear, and they are drawn inside the layout so they do not
  shift the page.
- Scrolling is not hijacked; anchors scroll smoothly only if the user asked for it.
- A list that changes while off-screen does not animate when it comes back.
- The cursor changes on the whole hit target, not just the label.


<!-- ===== skills/gatekeeper/SKILL.md ===== -->
---
name: gatekeeper
description: >-
  The audit layer: measure a finished render, page or asset against named gates, then look at it
  with fresh eyes before anyone else does. Use whenever work is about to be called done,
  presented, published or handed over — and whenever reviewing someone else's cut, design or
  animation. Turns "looks good to me" into named checks with numbers, and produces the ranked
  fix list when they fail.
license: MIT
---

# Gatekeeper

Every other skill in this suite makes judgements. This one checks them.

Two things never happen without passing through here: a render being presented, and
a piece being called complete. Not because the checks are profound, but because
**a completed render is not a correct render**, and the gap between those two is
where every embarrassing result lives.

## The nine gates

All commands below use `$SV` for the engine:

```bash
SV=/absolute/path/to/motionframe-edit/tools/mfe.py   # set once; resolved in skills/motionframe-edit/SKILL.md
```

```bash
python3 "$SV" gate --file out/final.mp4 --edl edl.json \
                   --boxes captions.boxes.json --out gate-report.json
```

| Gate | Name | Passes when | Measured by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G0** | render exists | decodes, non-blank, duration within 1% (or 0.35 s) of the plan, audio present | `mfe gate` |
| **G1** | delivery shape | exact width×height and fps for the profile; correct codec, container, pixel format | `mfe gate` |
| **G2** | loudness | integrated within ±2 LU of target, true peak ≤ −1 dBTP | `mfe gate` (ebur128) |
| **G3** | picture alive | no freeze > 0.5 s, no stretch > 3 s with no visual change | `mfe gate` (freezedetect + frame deltas) |
| **G4** | no black holes | no unintended black interval > 0.15 s | `mfe gate` |
| **G5** | cuts don't pop | no boundary spike > 6 dB over the local body level in the 120 ms around a cut | `mfe gate` (astats) |
| **G6** | captions safe | every cue box inside the platform safe zone; text height ≥ 3.5% of frame | `mfe gate` + boxes |
| **G7** | honest proof | every asset declares an origin; nothing generated claims to be real | `mfe gate` + `provenance.json` |
| **G8** | pace | no stretch over 3.5 s without a visible change, for anything under 90 s | `mfe gate` (scene detection) |

For pages, UIs and stills, the analogue is named and binary — see
`references/gates-for-design.md`. Same principle: no gate, no verdict.

## The audit, in order

The order is the cost order. Fixing a broken render after redesigning a section
wastes the redesign.

```
1  MEASURE     run the gates. Write the report to disk, not to the chat.
2  LOOK        contact sheet, then full-speed playback of the first 3 s and the last 3 s.
3  READ        describe every sheet frame in one sentence before judging it.
4  ROAST       a critic pass in fresh context, briefed to find problems. (references/critic.md)
5  FIX         in the fix order below. Re-run the gates. Cap at three passes.
6  REPORT      pass/fail per gate, plus what you could not check.
```

```bash
python3 "$SV" sheet --file out/final.mp4 --out work/sheet.jpg --every 1.5
```

**Describe before you judge.** One sentence per frame: what is on screen, what is
the hero, would this frame pass as a slide? Skipping this step is why people
"look" at a render for ten minutes and miss that the caption is behind the logo.

## 2b. The design read — required for anything that moves

The nine gates measure engineering. None of them can see that a frame has four typefaces, an
accent colour doing five jobs, or a chart with no labels. For a video or motion artifact, the
gate report is not finished until this is done:

```
python3 tools/mfe.py sheet --file <render> --out work/sheet.jpg --every 1
```

Then open the sheet and answer these, in this order, out loud:

1. **Type** — how many families? More than two (or two that are not a matched pair) fails D3.
   Is the caption the *weakest* text in the frame? It is the most-read text, so it cannot be.
2. **Colour** — name what the accent colour is doing. One meaning is a system; five meanings
   (numbers, arrows, chart lines, icons, annotations) is decoration.
3. **Legibility** — would every line survive being watched on a phone at arm's length? Grey on
   black at 40% is not a caption, it is a texture.
4. **Decoration test** — for each graphic: what does the viewer know after it that they did not
   know before? If the answer is the same number they just heard, cut it.
5. **Self-reference** — is the frame labelling itself (`SAMPLE 01`, `TAKE 3`, version numbers)?
   That is `anti-slop` 18. Remove it.

Write the answers into the report under **Design read**. A report without it is not a report
for motion work, it is a file probe.

## The fix order

Never fix in the order you noticed things. Fix in this order:

```
1  broken or untrue      (won't play, wrong claim, fabricated asset)
2  the idea              (there is no reason to watch)
3  connections           (beats don't hand off; sections don't follow)
4  hierarchy and scale   (the eye lands wrong; text unreadable at size)
5  timing                (too fast, too slow, dead stretch)
6  surface and finish    (grade, grain, borders, alignment)
7  sound polish          (last, because it is the cheapest to change and the
                          first thing people redo instead of the real problem)
```

## What you must report

A verdict is not a report. Every handoff includes:

- **Per-gate status**, with the number it was judged on.
- **The one warning you decided to keep**, and why it is acceptable.
- **What you could not check** — you cannot hear the mix, you cannot feel the
  timing on a phone, you cannot see it on a device you do not have. Say it.
- **The five fixes to do first**, if it failed. Ranked, with evidence.

Never: "audio looks good", "the design is clean", "should be fine now". If you did
not measure it, say you did not measure it.

## Three failure modes of the auditor

1. **The vacuous gate.** A check that cannot fail is decoration. Prove your gates
   can fail: `mfe demo --selftest` deliberately feeds broken renders to G2, G3, G1,
   G6 and G7 and asserts they trip. Do the same for any check you add.
2. **The infinite audit.** Three passes, then report. Past three, you are no longer
   improving the piece; you are avoiding the handoff.
3. **The polite critic.** A critic briefed to find good things will find them. Brief
   for the roast, and require timecodes and numbers as evidence.

## When a gate cannot pass

Some gates are legitimately unsatisfiable — a source with no audio, a platform
that demands 4:3, a brand that forbids the caption position that is readable.

Do not fake the number, and do not silently skip the gate. Instead:

> "G2 cannot pass: the source has no audio track and there is no music budget. I
> have delivered it silent with a note on the thumbnail. G0, G1, G3–G7 pass."

A stated, justified exception is professional. A silent one is the thing this
entire repository exists to prevent.

## Files

- `references/critic.md` — the fresh-context review brief
- `references/gates-for-design.md` — the binary checks for pages, UIs and stills
- `references/report-format.md` — the exact handoff format


<!-- ===== skills/gatekeeper/references/critic.md ===== -->
# The critic brief

A fresh-context review is the cheapest quality gain available, and it only works if
you brief it to attack. A critic asked "how does this look?" will say something
nice. A critic asked "find what is wrong, with evidence" will find it.

## Spawn it in a clean context

Give the critic: the rendered file, the EDL or design spec, the brief, and any
reference the user supplied. **Do not** give it your reasoning, your notes, or the
problems you already suspect — a fresh eye that inherits your blind spots is not a
fresh eye.

## The brief

```
You are reviewing a <type> piece for publication. Assume it is not good enough
yet and your job is to find out why. Do not praise. Do not be polite. Be specific.

INPUTS
  file            <path>
  spec            <edl.json | storyboard.md | design tokens>
  brief           <what it is for, who it is for, where it publishes>
  reference       <what the user asked it to feel like, if anything>

METHOD
  1  Look at the contact sheet and describe every frame in one sentence.
  2  Watch the first 3 seconds and the last 3 seconds at full speed.
  3  Then judge in this order: is it broken or untrue → is there a reason to
     watch → do the beats connect → does the eye land right → is the timing
     right → is the surface right → is the sound right.

OUTPUT  (exactly this shape, no preamble)
  VERDICT     one line — ship / fix first / rebuild
  PROBLEMS    ranked, each as: <severity> <timecode or element> <what is wrong>
              <the evidence you saw or measured> <the fix, in one line>
  FIRST FIVE  the five fixes that would move it furthest, in the order to do them
  DO NOT TOUCH  what is genuinely working, so the author does not break it
```

Require **evidence**: a timecode, a frame number, a measured level, an element
name. "The pacing feels off" is not a finding; "cuts at 0:04, 0:06 and 0:08 are
all 1.9 s with identical framing — the middle third has no rhythm change" is.

## What critics reliably catch that authors do not

- A payoff line cut half a word early.
- Captions that are legible on a laptop and not at phone size.
- The first 0.5 s doing nothing (no change, no claim, no sound).
- Audio that is 6 dB quieter than everything else the user publishes.
- Two elements with equal visual weight where one should lead.
- A section that restates the section before it.
- Text under a platform UI element.
- An ending that stops rather than closes.

## What to do with the output

- Take the top five, in the order given. Do not cherry-pick the easy one.
- If the critic and your own judgement disagree, the one with evidence wins.
- If the critic is wrong, write down why in `notes.md` — a critic that is
  systematically wrong about your project needs different input next time.
- Never present the critic's raw output to the user as your verdict. Synthesise:
  you are the supervisor, not the messenger.


<!-- ===== skills/gatekeeper/references/gates-for-design.md ===== -->
# Gates for design and stills

The video gates are measured by a script. These are judged by eye, but they are
**binary** — no sliding scale, no "mostly fine". Either the check passes or the
piece is not done. Nine of them, and a piece that fails three is a rebuild, not a
patch.

| Gate | Check | How to test |
|---|---|---|
| **D0** | Every visual renders | screenshots at 1440, 1024, 768, 390 — no empty frames, no placeholder boxes |
| **D1** | Legibility | body ≥ 16 px; contrast ≥ 4.5:1 body, ≥ 3:1 large and UI borders; nothing under 12 px |
| **D2** | Hierarchy | squint at 120 px: can you tell what is being sold, and what to do? |
| **D3** | One system | one type scale, one accent with one meaning, one spacing step, one radius family; no raw values in components |
| **D4** | Specificity | swap the logo for a competitor's — does the page still work? If yes, fail |
| **D5** | Content reality | no invented number, quote, logo, address, testimonial, screenshot; every asset declares an origin |
| **D6** | States | empty, loading, error, one item, 1000 items, 40-char unbroken text, missing fields, offline |
| **D7** | Accessibility | focus visible on every interactive element; `prefers-reduced-motion` respected; no information in colour or motion alone |
| **D8** | The one deviation | exactly one unexpected move against a quiet system. Zero is plain; two is noise |

## Why these and not "does it look nice"

"Nice" is not checkable, so it is not a gate. Each of the nine above can be
answered yes or no by someone who did not make the piece, which is the only
definition of a gate that matters.

## Fast procedure

```
1  Screenshot all four widths. Look at all four, at 100%, not zoomed out.
2  Squint / shrink to 120 px. One sentence: what is this selling?
3  Grep for raw values:  #[0-9a-f]{3,6}   [0-9]+px   [0-9]+ms
   Every hit outside the token file is a D3 failure.
4  Tab through the page. Is focus visible on every stop?
5  Force the states: rename the data, empty the list, break the image URL.
6  Turn on reduced motion. Does anything become invisible or unusable?
7  Read the copy aloud. Any sentence a competitor could also say?
```

## Report format

```
D0 pass  — 1440/1024/768/390, all visuals render
D1 pass  — body 17px, contrast 7.1:1
D2 fail  — at 120px it reads as "software"; the product is not visible above the fold
D3 pass  — 0 raw values outside tokens.css
D4 fail  — competitor-swap test passes: copy is category-level, not specific
D5 pass  — 1 image, origin declared
D6 warn  — empty and error states exist; 1000-item state untested
D7 pass  — focus visible, reduced motion honoured
D8 warn  — no deviation; the page is correct and forgettable
```

Two failures and one warning is a real verdict. It is also a plan.


<!-- ===== skills/gatekeeper/references/report-format.md ===== -->
# Report format

The handoff is the product. Two artifacts, both short, both factual.

## 1. `report.md` — for the human publishing it

```markdown
# <piece> — 52 s, 1080×1920

**Shape**         hook → claim → proof → turn → CTA
**Take choices**  s3 (2nd take of the opening), s7 (last, cleanest)
**Cut**           11 segments · 40–120 ms padding · cuts on silences ≥ 400 ms
**Grade**         neutral_punch, +6 sat, no hue shift
**Captions**      bold-pop · 34 cues · active-word accent · 9 names proofread
**Sound**         −14.2 LUFS · TP −1.3 dBTP · music −19 dB under voice · 4 SFX
**Gates**         G0–G2, G4–G8 pass · G3 warn (intentional 1.2 s hold before payoff)
**Not checked**   the mix on a phone speaker
**Open**          the third stat needs a real source before publishing
```

Nothing else. No process notes, no self-congratulation, no restating the brief.

## 2. `gate-report.json` — for the machine and the next session

Produced by `mfe gate`. Keep it in the output folder. It is how a future session
knows what was already verified, and it is the only proof that anything was
audited at all.

```json
{
  "tool": "motionframe-edit 1.0.0",
  "file": "out/final.mp4",
  "profile": "vertical-9x16",
  "media": { "duration_s": 52.1, "display_width": 1080, "display_height": 1920, "fps": 30 },
  "gates": [ { "id": "G2", "name": "loudness", "status": "pass",
               "detail": "-14.2 LUFS (target -14±2), true peak -1.3 dBTP" } ],
  "verdict": "pass",
  "warnings": 1
}
```

## The sentence that must never be missing

Every handoff ends with the thing you could not verify:

> "I can't hear the mix — check that the music sits under the voice on a phone
> speaker. Everything else is measured."

You are not allowed to imply you checked something you did not. That single
sentence is what separates motionframe-edit from a confident guess.


<!-- ===== skills/taste-memory/SKILL.md ===== -->
---
name: taste-memory
description: >-
  Turn corrections into durable rules so the next piece starts where the last one finished. Use
  when the user gives feedback on a result, says "I hate X" or "always do Y", when a project has
  a taste.md, or when starting new work in a project that has been worked on before. Stops the
  same note being given twice.
license: MIT
---

# Taste memory

The reason people keep twenty skills open in a chat is not that no single skill has
the knowledge. It is that **none of them remember anything**. Every session starts
from the median and gets corrected back to the same place.

This is the smallest skill in the suite and the one that changes the most.

## The file

`taste.md` lives at the project root, created by `mfe scaffold`. It is read **before**
any decision and appended to **after** every correction.

```markdown
# Taste — this person's corrections, in their own words

## Global
- No music beds on talking-head pieces. Silence is fine. (replaced: a −22 dB bed)
- End holds ≤ 1.2 s. (replaced: 2.0 s default)

## Pacing
- Cuts land 60 ms after the last word, not 100. (replaced: 30–200 ms guidance, tighter)
- Keep one 1.5 s still before the payoff. (replaced: cutting every gap)

## Captions
- Never ALL CAPS. (replaced: bold-pop default)
- No accent colour on captions, at all. (replaced: active-word accent)

## Sound
- Music ducked to inaudibility under speech, then up 4 dB between sentences.
- No whooshes on cuts. Ever.

## Look
- Grade is neutral; no teal shadows. (replaced: warm_cinematic)

## Never
- Generated images of people.
- Emoji anywhere in a video.
```

## How to write a rule

A rule has three parts, and all three matter:

1. **The instruction, in the user's terms.** "No music beds" — not
   "music_gain_db: none".
2. **What it replaced**, so a future reader knows which default lost.
3. **The scope** — the heading. A caption rule is not a pacing rule.

Bad: `- music: false` (unreadable in three weeks)
Good: `- No music on talking heads. Silence is fine. (replaced: a −22 dB bed)`

## The loop

```
read taste.md          at the start, before the brief, before the footage
  ↓
make the piece
  ↓
take the note          "the end is too long" — as a note, not a setting
  ↓
write the rule         instruction + what it replaced, under the right heading
  ↓
say it back            one line: "End holds now cap at 1.2 s. Noted for next time."
```

The say-back matters: it tells the user the note is durable, which is why they stop
repeating themselves.

## What is a rule and what is not

| Note | Rule? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "this thumbnail is great" | **no** | a one-off |
| "always pick the more graphic thumbnail" | yes — Look | a preference with direction |
| "cut the second stat" | no | a content decision for this piece |
| "I never want stats in the first 5 s" | yes — Pacing | generalisable |
| "this client's brand is green" | yes — but in `brief.md` | project fact, not taste |
| "use a different font for this" | **ask once**: this piece, or always? | ambiguity is the only time to ask |

The test: **would saying it again next session be annoying?** If yes, it is a rule.

## Rewriting versus appending

Append. Never rewrite history, because a reversal is information:

```markdown
- Captions in caps. (replaced: sentence case, 2026-03)
- Back to sentence case — caps felt shouty at 45 s. (replaced: caps)
```

Two lines that contradict each other, in date order, tell the truth. One line that
silently changed tells a lie about what the person wanted.

## When taste contradicts the laws

Taste outranks style, never correctness or legibility. If a rule would break a law
(captions under the UI, a pop at every cut, a fabricated screenshot), say so once:

> "You asked for captions at the bottom edge. On Reels that is exactly where the
> caption bar sits, so the words will be covered. I've put them 40 px higher and
> noted the reason. Say the word and I'll move them back."

Then follow the instruction, and note the exception in the file.

## Portability

`taste.md` is plain markdown with no schema beyond headings. Copy it between
projects, keep a `global/` version for a person and a per-project one for a client,
and read the specific before the general. It should still be readable in five
years, by a human, without this skill installed.

# The library — eighteen sources, combined

This folder is the combination. Every source in the brief is here, and how it is here
depends on its licence — not on convenience:

| Mode | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **copy** | The licence permits redistribution. Files copied verbatim under `upstream/`, the
|  | upstream LICENCE travelling alongside as `LICENCE.upstream`. |
| **copy-permission** | The licence does *not* permit redistribution, but the maintainer states they
|  | have permission from the rights holder. Copied verbatim, with `PERMISSION.md` recording the
|  | basis, the date, and that no licence grant is verifiable from upstream. |

**All 18 sources copied · 1824 files · 13,419,822 bytes.** 14 under a licence grant, 0 on asserted permission.

## How the skills use it

`skills/` is the merge — one voice, contradictions settled. `library/` is the evidence:
the source material to check that merge against, loaded only when a job needs the depth.
That is progressive disclosure, and it is what lets eighteen sources fit into one install.

## Editorial notes

Each source folder also carries `NOTES.md` where one exists: what that source is good at,
what it gets wrong, and where its rules landed in `skills/`. Notes are this project's
writing, not the upstream's.

## What is not here

- **Assets** — themes, fonts, images, example films. Licences vary and a skill repo is not
  an asset dump.
- **Applications** — `open-edit`'s CLI code and `hypit`'s workflow are tools; only their
  doctrine is useful here.
- **Contradictions** — left as contradictions in the sources, resolved in
  `../skills/motionframe-edit/references/precedence.md`, and nowhere else.

<!-- ===== specs/quality-bar.md ===== -->
# The quality bar, as a contract

The bar is written down so that it cannot be quietly lowered — by a model, by a tired
author, or by a reviewer who wants to ship. **addyosmani/agent-skills** calls this
constraint-driven development; here it is executable wherever possible.

## What "done" means

A piece is done when **all** of the following are true. Not "mostly". Not "except the audio".

| # | Condition | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | It exists as a file and decodes | gate G0 |
| 2 | It has the exact shape the destination requires | gate G1 |
| 3 | Its loudness is within ±2 LU of target, true peak ≤ −1 dBTP | gate G2 |
| 4 | Nothing freezes for >0.5 s, nothing is still for >3 s unless intended | gate G3 |
| 5 | No unintended black interval | gate G4 |
| 6 | No boundary spike >6 dB over the local body level | gate G5 |
| 7 | Every caption cue is inside the platform safe zone | gate G6 |
| 8 | Every asset declares an origin; nothing generated claims to be real | gate G7 |

Run `mfe gate --file <render> --edl <edl.json>` and the report says PASS or FAIL with
numbers. A human "looks fine" is not one of the conditions.

## What "good" means

Correctness is gateable; judgement is not. These are the judgement conditions, and they are
checked by a critic with fresh eyes (`gatekeeper/references/critic.md`):

1. **It has one point** and says it in the first two seconds.
2. **One system**: one type scale, one palette, one motion register.
3. **Nothing is on screen that is not carrying information.**
4. **The cut serves the audio**, not the other way round.
5. **The first version of the idea that works** — not the third, not the safest.
6. **A stranger can say what it was about** after one watch.

## What is never acceptable, at any speed

- A paid dependency, an API key, or an account in the happy path.
- A generated image presented as a real capture.
- A render presented as finished that has not passed its gates.
- A claim in the repository that cannot be checked.
- Copying another project's text or assets where its licence does not allow it.

## How the bar is enforced on this repository

`tools/gate-docs.py` applies the same discipline to the repository itself — links,
frontmatter, generated drift, unfinished text, superlatives without evidence, provenance —
and `--selftest` feeds each gate broken input to prove it can fail. CI runs it on every
push, along with the engine tests, the installer check, and the end-to-end self-audit.

A gate that cannot fail is decoration.


<!-- ===== docs/plan.md ===== -->
# Status, and what is not finished

This project is a first release, not a finished product. This page lists what is known to be
unfinished or weak, in the order it matters, so nobody has to discover it by accident.

## Known gaps

**1. Renders are validated against a synthetic fixture, not real footage.**
`mfe.py demo --selftest` builds a test clip with known defects — a freeze, a silent stretch, a
wrong aspect — and proves the gates catch them. That tests the gates, not your camera. On real
footage, expect to correct frame-rate and rotation mismatches the fixture never produces.

**2. Rule-level tracing is partial.**
`docs/absorption.md` maps each source to the files in `skills/` that carry its capability. That
is a topic-level map. Only one source has been traced at the level of individual rules
(`i-hate-editing`, in `skills/edit-supervisor/references/cutting.md`), where five rules the
earlier draft missed were added. Until the rest are done, "combined" is a claim about ideas,
not a line-by-line audit.

**3. Loudness and safe zones are measured; whether the edit is any good is not.**
The gates check duration, aspect, loudness, freeze, black, cut boundaries, caption placement
and asset provenance. None of them can tell you the pacing is wrong.

**4. Four sources are here on the maintainer's stated permission.**
`hypit`, `remotion`, `apple-design` and the TikTok short-edit document do not grant
redistribution. Their folders record the basis in `PERMISSION.md`. If you are redistributing
this repository further, read `NOTICE` first — the MIT licence does not cover them.

**5. One motion lane has its own licence.**
Remotion is free only below a company-size threshold. It is optional: the other two lanes
(HTML + GSAP + headless Chrome, and ffmpeg alone) carry no such condition.

**6. No Windows-native testing.**
CI runs Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13 on Linux. `install.sh` is POSIX shell; on Windows it
assumes WSL or Git Bash. Nobody has tested PowerShell.

## What would move this forward

1. **Finish the rule-level audit** for the other seventeen sources, in the format used for
   `i-hate-editing`: every rule in the source, marked covered or missing, missing ones written.
2. **Run the gates on real footage** from three cameras with different rotation metadata, and
   record where they disagree with a human reviewer.
3. **Windows check** on a fresh machine, then either support it or say plainly that it is
   unsupported.

## How to see the current state for yourself

```bash
python3 tools/gate-docs.py          # the repository's own documentation checks
python3 tools/absorb.py --check      # all 18 sources present, each with its licence basis
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
```

CI runs all three on every push, plus a clean-machine install.


<!-- ===== docs/architecture.md ===== -->
# Architecture

## The split that makes it work

The skills hold judgement; the tools hold measurement. The skills decide what should happen
and why. `tools/mfe.py` does the parts that can be checked by a machine — probing, cutting,
captioning, measuring — and hands back numbers rather than opinions. Nothing crosses that line
in both directions: prose never asserts a duration or a loudness figure it did not get from a
command.

Most skill repos are all judgement: strong opinions, no verification. The result
is confident work with defects nobody caught. This project puts every checkable
claim into an executable, and leaves prose responsible only for the things that
cannot be measured — taste, hierarchy, rhythm, whether an idea is worth making.

**Rule of thumb:** if a claim can be verified, it belongs in `mfe.py` or a gate. If
it lives only in prose, it is a suggestion, and it will be skipped under pressure.

## Data flow

```
footage ──▶ probe ──▶ transcript (word-level, cached)
                          │
                          ├──▶ packed reading view  ──▶ EDL (the contract)
                          │                                │
                          │             ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                          │             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
                          │        segments           captions           overlays
                          │        (extract,          (remapped to        (PTS-shifted,
                          │         fade, scale,       output time)        frame 0 at `at`)
                          │         speed)                 │                  │
                          │             └──────────┬────────┴──────────────────┘
                          │                        ▼
                          │                 composite: overlays → captions LAST → loudnorm
                          │                        │
                          │                        ▼
                          │                  gate_report() ──▶ gate-report.json
                          │                        │
                          └────────────────────────┴──▶ contact sheet + report.md + provenance.json
```

## Four decisions worth defending

**1. The EDL is the single source of truth.**
Every artifact is derived: captions, overlays, sound, notes, variants, gates. It
is JSON so a machine can validate it, small enough to read, and human-editable
when a human wants to nudge something. A tool that renders without an EDL cannot
be re-timed, re-graded or audited cheaply, which is why the sources that do it
that way also cannot fix drift.

**2. Two encodes, not six.**
Per-segment extract (with grade, fades, speed, scale) → lossless concat → one
composite pass that does overlays, captions and loudness together. Adding an
overlay must never re-encode every segment, and captions must never be applied
before overlays. Both of those are silent failures in the wild; here they are
structural.

**3. Output time is the only time.**
`sources → segments → output` is a coordinate change, and captions/overlays/notes
must be authored in the output space. `remap_words_to_output()` is the only
sanctioned conversion. This one design choice eliminates the most common
class of defect in assembled cuts.

**4. Gates return data, not vibes.**
`gate_report()` returns JSON: per-gate status, the number judged, and the facts
behind it. That is what makes `mfe demo --selftest` possible — you cannot feed a
vibe a broken render and assert it notices.

## Progressive disclosure

```
skills/motionframe-edit/SKILL.md      ~150 lines   always loaded
  └─ references/precedence.md          ~120 lines   loaded when rules conflict
  └─ references/lineage.md             ~130 lines   loaded when provenance matters
skills/edit-supervisor/SKILL.md        ~200 lines   loaded when editing footage
  └─ references/cutting.md             ~140 lines
  └─ references/captions.md            ~90 lines
  └─ references/sound.md               ~80 lines
  └─ references/delivery.md            ~90 lines
```

A 3,000-line monolith would be one skill that reliably evicts itself from context
halfway through the work. The split means a captioning task loads the router plus
one reference file — about 400 lines — instead of everything.

## Degradation, not substitution

Every optional capability has a defined fallback, and the engine reports which one
is active rather than failing silently:

| Missing | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| ffprobe | parse `ffmpeg -i` for duration, streams and rotation |
| ASR | refuse to guess; ask for a transcript or an SRT, and say why |
| libass | `mfe captions` still writes a valid `.ass`; burning needs libass |
| Node / Chrome | the HTML/React lanes are unavailable; the ffmpeg lane still works |
| fonts | warn; captions render in a fallback face with a different metric |

The one substitution that never happens is a paid API. If a capability is absent,
the answer is "this is unavailable, here is the free path", never a silent upload.

## Extending

- **New destination** (a platform with a new aspect): add a profile to
  `PROFILES` in `tools/mfe.py` and a row to the table in
  `skills/edit-supervisor/references/delivery.md`.
- **New gate**: add it to `gate_report()`, to `specs/gates.json`, to the table in
  `skills/gatekeeper/SKILL.md`, and to the selftest with a fixture it must catch.
- **New render lane**: document it in `skills/motion-director/references/lanes.md`
  and make it optional. Nothing may require it.
- **New style**: add a `CAPTION_STYLES` entry or a named grade preset; never a
  parallel code path.


<!-- ===== docs/platforms.md ===== -->
# Platforms

One source of truth (`AGENTS.md` + `skills/`), many entry points. Nothing here is
duplicated per platform; the adapters are pointers, which is why they cannot drift.

| Agent | What it reads | Install |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code / Claude** | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter, discovered in `~/.claude/skills/` | `./install.sh --target claude` |
| **ChatGPT / Codex** | `AGENTS.md` at the repo root (hierarchy-walked); shared skills in `~/.codex/skills/` if your build supports them | `./install.sh --target codex` |
| **Gemini CLI** | `GEMINI.md` context file + `gemini-extension.json` | `gemini extensions link .` |
| **Antigravity** | `AGENTS.md`; skills convention `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/` | `./install.sh --target antigravity` |
| **OpenCode** | `AGENTS.md`; skills in `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/opencode/skills/` | `./install.sh --target opencode` |
| **Hermes / Cursor / Windsurf / Zed / Aider / anything else** | `AGENTS.md` | `./install.sh --dir <your skills dir>`, or set `MFE_SKILLS_DIR` |

## The three ways to mount it

**1. Skills directory (best).** The agent discovers each skill by its `description`
and loads a body only when it routes there. This is progressive disclosure, and it
is why the suite is seven skills rather than one enormous file.

```bash
./install.sh --target claude          # symlinks all seven into ~/.claude/skills
./install.sh --dir ~/my/agent/skills  # anywhere else
./install.sh --copy                   # for filesystems where symlinks fail
```

**2. Single context file (always works).** Every tool in the table can read a
markdown file. Paste or reference `AGENTS.md`, and point at the router:

```
Read AGENTS.md, then skills/motionframe-edit/SKILL.md before starting. Load other
skills from skills/<name>/SKILL.md only when the routing table says to.
```

**3. Project-local (per client, per repo).** Drop a project's `taste.md`,
`brief.md` and `edl.json` next to the footage and let the agent read those first.
This is how a one-off becomes a house style.

## Paths, honestly

Agent skill directories move as tooling matures. If your tool reads skills from a
path that is not listed above, do not edit `install.sh` — override it:

```bash
MFE_SKILLS_DIR=~/.my-agent/skills ./install.sh
```

If a target prints a path that does not exist on your machine, that is expected:
the installer creates it, and the list above records the convention this repo
targets, not a guarantee about any particular build.

## What each platform gets

- **Claude Code**: the richest experience — real skills, subagents for parallel
  beats, hooks for a pre-delivery gate. `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` makes it
  installable as a plugin.
- **Codex / ChatGPT**: `AGENTS.md` plus skills where supported. Codex is strongest
  at the engine work (`mfe.py`) because it can run commands in a loop and read the
  gate report.
- **Gemini CLI / Antigravity**: the extension manifest gives it `GEMINI.md` as
  context. Good at long-reference reading (`docs/lineage.md`, the lane docs).
- **OpenCode / Hermes / others**: `AGENTS.md` is the contract. Everything else is
  plain markdown, and the engine is a single stdlib file — it will work.

## The rule that keeps this portable

No skill depends on a platform feature. Subagents are an optimisation, not a
requirement: everything here can be done serially by one model with a shell. That
is deliberate, because the day a specific skill format changes, the doctrine is
still readable and the engine still runs.
